antirequisites: N/A

title: Maths for Machine Learning
overview: This course aims to equip students with mathematical skills critical for understanding and applying machine learning algorithms. Students will be able to explain and apply the mathematical concepts essential for machine learning, focusing on calculus, linear algebra, optimisation, probability, and information theory. Essential for machine learning and data science curricula, this course strengthens mathematical foundations, supporting advanced studies and practical applications in the field.
learning_outcomes: Apply techniques from linear algebra to solve problems involving vectors and matrices
Formulate and solve problems using multivariable functions and derivatives
Perform computations with random variables, probabilities and entropy
Use Python to verify solutions and produce solutions for more complex problems
Present results of calculations in a clear and logical manner
prerequisites: Must have completed MATH1000 Foundations in Mathematics OR must have completed SACE Stage 2 Mathematical Methods or equivalent
antirequisites: N/A
assessment: Short Response Questions, Short Response Questions, Short Response Questions, Short Response Questions, Short Response Questions, Short Response Questions, Short Response Questions, Short Response Questions, Short Response Questions – 10%

title: Artificial Intelligence
overview: This course aims to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of artificial intelligence (AI), focusing on its key sub-areas and applications. Students will learn the fundamentals of agent-based artificial intelligence systems and their fundamental underlying search-based methods for decision-making and optimisation. Students will design and develop practical systems based existing AI technologies. This course equips students with practical skills in AI, preparing them for more advanced studies.
learning_outcomes: Describe key milestones, AI concepts and the components of intelligent agents to technical and non-technical audiences
Describe the core principles and technologies underpinning sub-areas such as computer vision, natural language processing and robotics, including their distinct functions and uses
Develop fundamental search-based algorithms and analyse their complexity, completeness, and optimality
Develop AI applications which leverage formalised logic and inference to solve problems
Explain the ethical and cultural considerations and societal implications of deploying artificial intelligence
prerequisites: Must have completed COMP1002 Problem Solving and Programming
antirequisites: Must not have completed ARTI2003 Artificial Intelligence

title: Cloud and Concurrent Programming
overview: This advanced course will equip students with high level skills to manage access to cloud based services whilst maintaining application-level data without corruption. In this course, students will have the opportunity to develop basic cloud and user level applications to solve user problems, and to review the ethical, legal and security considerations of building applications dependant on cloud services. On the user side, the course will enable students to model concurrent applications including writing multi-threaded applications to support safe access to cloud platforms. Students will be able to build thread safe endpoint applications that leverage cloud-based services to provide solutions for modern user requirements.
learning_outcomes: Implement threading and synchronisation correctly in a high-level language supporting concurrency.
Construct safe high performance parallel and concurrent software using sound theoretical techniques.
Design and build cloud-based applications that provide web services and use web APIs in their implementation.
Build complex applications that safely integrate concurrency with web services to create high performance solutions that are resistant to deadlocks and timeouts.
Design and build privacy and security compliant applications that utilise web-based APIs.
prerequisites: Must have completed all of COMP1003 Structured Data/COMP2021 Software Development Practice
antirequisites: Must not have completed INFT3043 Cloud and Concurrent Programming at the University of South Australia

title: Machine Learning
overview: This course provides a foundational understanding of machine learning, covering its core concepts, mathematical foundations, and diverse applications. By the end of the course, learners will be able to understand and implement basic machine learning algorithms and evaluate the algorithms on a variety of datasets using suitable evaluation metrics. This course prepares students to effectively apply machine learning techniques to real-world problems and sets the foundation for more advanced studies in machine learning and artificial intelligence.
learning_outcomes: Describe key concepts in machine learning and their advantages and disadvantages in various applications
Demonstrate the principles of simple machine learning algorithms and models including Linear Regression, Naive Bayes, SVM, K-Nearest Neighbour and Decision Trees
Evaluate simple machine learning algorithms on both synthetic and real-world datasets using appropriate evaluation metrics
Apply data preparation techniques to clean, preprocess, and transform data for machine learning tasks

antirequisites: Must not have completed ARTI2001 Machine Learning

title: Data Structures and Algorithms
overview: Building knowledge of how algorithms and data structures, such as arrays, lists, queues, stacks, trees and graphs, can be used to implement efficient software solutions. Learning the basic principles of assessing computational complexity of algorithms. Students will also learn to select appropriate data structures and algorithms for solving problems, taking into consideration time and space requirements.

Discuss factors that influence the choice of data structures
Implement algorithms to solve problems
Discuss the selection of an algorithm including any selection criteria
Use recursion to solve problems

antirequisites: Must not have completed INFS2042 Data Structures Advanced at the University of South Australia OR must not have completed COMPSCI2103 Algorithm Design & Data Structures for Engineers at the University of Adelaide

title: Professional Communication and Teamwork
overview: This course enables students to develop skills in professional communication, teamwork, ethics, project management, and IT governance to prepare them for effective ICT practice. This course equips students with essential skills and knowledge to communicate effectively, collaborate in teams, and uphold ethical and professional standards in ICT practice. It explores principles of professional communication, teamwork, and leadership, along with key aspects of project management and IT governance. Through practical applications and case studies, students will develop the competencies required to navigate complex professional environments and contribute to successful ICT projects.

Analyse ethical issues in ICT and privacy and security concerns, using established ethical frameworks and industry standards, and incorporate cultural sensitivities into ICT projects.
Apply best practices for teamwork and conflict resolution techniques to collaborate within diverse ICT projects.
Discuss the responsibilities, expectations, and professional standards of ICT practitioners, adhering to codes of conduct, industry practices and legal requirements.
Apply fundamental PMBOK project management principles to ICT projects.
Explain key IT governance frameworks and compliance requirements, and their impact on ICT decision-making and organisational success.

Present results and recommendations to stakeholders

antirequisites: Must not have completed ARTIX300 Neural Networks and Deep Learning

title: Advanced Data Structures and Algorithms
overview: Building upon prior knowledge on basic data structures and algorithms, this course aims to elevate students sound theoretical understanding and practical skills for solving complex problems using advanced data structures and algorithms. The course will strengthen sound theoretical knowledge on computational complexity and proving validity of algorithms. Advanced data structures such as self-balancing trees, graphs, maps and hash maps, will be explained, along with their relevant algorithms, as well as advanced approaches to problem solving. Learners will gain and strengthen their knowledge and skills to solve complex problems by applying and building advanced data structures and algorithms.

Demonstrate the validity of advanced algorithms in solving complex problems
Evaluate the complexity of data structures and algorithms in solving complex problems
Develop software solutions by applying advanced data structures and algorithms

title: ICT Capstone Project 2

title: Grand Challenges
overview: This course will introduce the key research areas in computer science and the challenges confronting the discipline. They will develop use an exploration of the grand challenges of computer science to learn key skills like logic, ethic and reasoning in order to build arguments and have well informed discussions. Students will leave the course with a strong understanding of the state of the computer science discipline and be able to eloquently make reasoned arguments on how to approach solving them.

Evaluate information using logical and rhetorical principles
Demonstrate teamwork and collaboration
Design a solution to an assigned problem in research or industry.
Evaluate a solution based on your design.
Produce written reports, presentations, and summaries of your work progress, team interaction, and results.

title: Statistics for Human Factors
overview: This course aims to equip students with essential statistical methods and analytical tools vital for human factors research. The focus is on developing robust understanding and skills in executing various statistical tests, from foundational concepts to advanced analysis techniques. By learning topics such as descriptive statistics, null hypothesis significance testing, programming with statistics software packages, data visualization, parametric and non-parametric methods, and advanced topics like regression, latent variable analysis, and General Linear Model, students will be prepared to conduct rigorous and meaningful research in human factors, ensuring they can effectively analyse data, and interpret results within real-world applications.
learning_outcomes: Describe fundamental statistical principles for human factor research.
Analyse the results from practical statistical tests commonly used in human factor research.

Examine research designs and data quality, using statistical techniques and measures to ensure research standards.

title: Interactive Systems Design
overview: This course equips learners with the human and technical design skills to create usable interactive systems. Modern interactive systems necessitates a tight coupling between the system feedback (the gulf of evaluation) and the interaction with underlying data, algorithms, and systems (the gulf of execution). Students will practice human centred design processes, usability factors, rapid prototyping, and techniques for reflecting on a design throughout the development process. Students will learn technical skills in architecture design of interactive systems, design patterns, and the use of open-source frameworks to create interactive systems. This course aligns with the program’s aim of designing and developing innovative solutions that demonstrate a high usability.
learning_outcomes: Discuss human centred design methodologies and associated principles for creating interactive systems.
Design the user interface of an interactive system that meet the needs of end-users.
Create real-time interactive systems using modern frameworks
Evaluate the quality attributes of an interactive system using methods.

title: Agile Development and User Experience
overview: This course equips students with the knowledge and skills needed to effectively apply Agile development principles using Scrum, along with Lean UX practices, to enhance the efficiency, collaboration, and user-centricity of software development projects. Participants will learn how to utilise Scrum practices and roles, as well as integrate Lean UX methodologies to streamline the design and development process. Students will also learn how to apply ethical frameworks and professional standards to project decisions and navigate difficult stakeholder interactions using professional communication and conflict management strategies. The course draws on project management principles to support the delivery of high-quality products that meet user needs and business objectives.
learning_outcomes: Apply Agile and Scrum methodologies to plan, execute, and iteratively deliver a team-based IT project, including backlog management, sprint planning, and retrospective analysis.
Demonstrate proficiency with Agile tools and practices, including story writing, estimation, velocity tracking, and stakeholder communication within the Scrum framework.
Design user experiences using Lean UX principles, incorporating iterative feedback and minimal viable product (MVP) thinking to drive customer-focused outcomes.
Employ established UX methods such as empathy mapping, persona creation, and usability evaluation to create accessible and effective user-centred designs.
Apply ethical frameworks and professional standards to assess project decisions involving user privacy, dark patterns, accessibility, and informed consent.

Manage difficult stakeholder interactions, including clients and team members, by applying professional communication strategies, conflict resolution techniques, and emotional regulation practices in a project setting.

overview: This course aims to provide students with a comprehensive introduction to the foundational research methods and measurement of human-computer interaction (HCI). It covers core concepts, principles, and methodologies, including user-centred design, usability evaluation, and interface prototyping. Students will learn how to apply these concepts to design effective user interfaces, enhance user experiences, and consider the ethical implications of design practices and products.

Apply HCI theories and models to analyze and inform system and interface design.

Students will engage in practical projects to develop interactive systems, gain experience in enhancing usability, and learn to critically assess the integration of AI in society, ensuring these technologies are both impactful and ethical.

Identify and address ethical and cultural concerns in AI design, ensuring systems promote fairness, transparency, and accountability

Employ concepts and methods from discrete mathematics in various applications
Demonstrate skills in mathematical communication
Demonstrate knowledge of discrete mathematical concepts and carry out calculations involving discrete structures

title: Theory of Computation and Formal Verification
overview: This course delves into the fundamental concepts of computability theory, exploring the boundaries and limitations of algorithmic solutions. Students will examine the classification of algorithmic solutions, studying various types of algorithms and their applicability to different problem domains. The course also covers formal verification techniques, providing learners with the tools to rigorously assess the correctness and reliability of algorithms. This formal lens will also be used to analyse and compare between software development practices.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate advanced knowledge of formal computation and its relationship to languages
Analyse different computing languages and classify their respective types
Describe formal reasoning about languages
Formalise specifications of various programs
Apply the inductive hypothesis in various settings
Analyse current software development practices through a formal lens
prerequisites: must have completed MATH1006 Discrete Mathematics
antirequisites: N/A

title: Cyber Security Application
overview: This course introduces students to real-world cyber security challenges faced by organisations. Students will apply cyber and computing knowledge and skills gained in previous courses to address these challenges in complex situations, producing advanced solutions. By merging theoretical understanding with practical application, students develop advanced strategies to mitigate cyber threats, safeguard sensitive information, and fortify organisational resilience in the face of evolving cyber risks.
learning_outcomes: Apply knowledge of operating systems, networking, and cybersecurity principles to perform security testing and implement solutions for real-world cybersecurity challenges.
Evaluate the effectiveness of cybersecurity solutions and controls using appropriate assessment techniques.
Analyse systems and applications to identify and assess cybersecurity vulnerabilities, threats, and risks.
Communicate cybersecurity findings and ethical, legal, and professional considerations
prerequisites: Must have completed 2 of COMP1005 Object-Oriented Programming, COMP1034/INFO1016 Security Foundations
antirequisites: N/A

title: Structures
overview: To develop students' analytical skills in understanding structural behaviour, distinguishing between different types of loads and describing different types of structural members. To introduce students to the analysis and design of simple building structures according to relevant codes and regulations to start collaborating with engineers and other professionals, utilising their analytical skills to address challenges in the construction industry at a foundational level.
learning_outcomes: Analyse, predict and think critically about the behaviour of elements in simple structures subjected to permanent, imposed, and other actions through building a small-scale structural model.

Select and apply mathematical procedures to analyse simple structures, including evaluating the loading based on relevant Australian Standards, calculating the support reactions, shear forces, normal forces, bending moments and deflections.
Prepare structural design for key structural members in a small-scale building using design capacity tables and determine costs.
Communicate structural concepts through mathematics, drawings, photographs, presentations and software.
antirequisites: Must not have completed CIVE 1002 - Structures 1 at University of South Australia

title: Construction Economics and Procurement
overview: The course aims to equip students with knowledge relating to the fundamentals of micro-economic and macro-economic theory as well as procurement methods used for construction projects. Upon successful completion of the course, students will have a fundamental understanding of how the national economy and construction sector is affected by the global economy and the government’s approach to monetary and fiscal policies. Students will also have a comprehensive understanding of the various methods used in the construction industry to procure construction services including construct only, design & construct, cost plus, remeasurement, management contracting, construction management, public private partnerships and alliance contracting. Overall, the course will improve students’ critical thinking and interpreting skills along with communication skills. This course aligns with the program’s intent of providing knowledge to commence professional practice in construction management disciplines.
learning_outcomes: Describe the economic characteristics of the construction industry
Describe fundamental micro-economic theory and relate it to firms in the construction industry
Discuss fundamental macroeconomic theory explaining the behaviour of construction output and its relationship to national economic output

Identify the various stages of the traditional construction project lifecycle and explain the key activities that take place at each stage including the roles of the construction stakeholders/professionals involved
Describe the traditional and novel project procurement methods commonly used in the construction industry
Appraise the suitability of procurement methods commonly used in the construction industry for various types of construction projects
antirequisites: Must not have completed BUIL 1023 Introduction to Construction Business Management at the University of South Australia

title: Construction Science and Materials
overview: This course aims to introduce students to common construction materials, including concrete, steel, timber, and masonry, and to environmental considerations within the built environment. It provides essential knowledge that underpins further learning in courses such as structures, construction management, and construction.
learning_outcomes: Understand the terminology, characteristics, and scientific and engineering properties of principal construction materials, along with other factors influencing their selection and performance
Identify and report on the appropriate and best practice application and installation requirements of construction materials and components
Demonstrate understanding of climate parameters and passive building designs for indoor environmental quality and energy efficiency
Explain the integration of renewable energy, water-efficient features, and noise control measures in buildings
Explore sustainable building innovations and communicate sustainability concepts to stakeholders
antirequisites: Must not have completed CONMGNT1000 at University of Adelaide and CIVE 1003, CIVE2008, CIVE1006 and CIVE 2015 at University of South Australia AND must not have completed  BLDG1006 UO Construction Materials/BLDG2008 UO Construction Environmental Science

title: Construction Communication and Digital Construction Fundamentals
overview: This course aims to provide learners with a deep understanding of communication tools in construction, integrating manual drafting, Revit, and BIM alongside ISO 19650 and RIBA Plan of Work. Through immersive experiences with virtual reality, students develop effective verbal, written, and visual communication skills, fostering teamwork and autonomy. emphasising problem-solving, ethical conduct, and sustainable development, learners cultivate critical thinking, research skills, and environmental awareness crucial for professional practice. The course addresses problem-solving, understanding others' needs, ethical actions, and effective communication, while fostering skills in communication, critical thinking, and technological competence.
learning_outcomes: Understanding the communication processes and core activities for traditional and digital construction projects based on the RIBA Plan of Work and the ISO 19650 standards to convey project information effectively across stakeholders with precision and alignment

Develop effective stakeholder engagement plans integrating verbal, written, and 2D drawings/3D visual communication skills for informed decision-making and progress monitoring throughout project lifecycles, ensuring comprehensive strategic alignment
Examine collaboration approaches among construction stakeholders, considering client needs and BIM advancements, to enhance productivity with a deep understanding and critical evaluation

Demonstrate proficient use of innovative technologies, especially BIM, in construction projects to achieve productivity, efficiency, and sustainability goals, while upholding ethical and legal standards
antirequisites: Must not have completed BUIL 1021 Construction Communication at the University of South Australia
assessment: Multiple Choice Questions, Multiple Choice Questions – 35%

title: High-rise Construction
overview: This course aims to equip students with the knowledge and skills on the construction of high-rise Buildings, and will cover an array of topics such as a history of tall buildings, their structural elements including wind and seismic loading's through to handling of materials, people movement within the building, de-construction, sustainability and modular high rise construction.
learning_outcomes: Have an in-depth understanding of the history and evolution of high-rise buildings.
Critically review multi-story construction methods and materials used for the construction of high-rise buildings.
Gain an understanding of building dead and live loads, as well as seismic and wind loads on tall buildings.
Evaluate the logistics involved in the construction of a building such as materials handling, and people movement and the methods of demolishing a high-rise building.
Explore the use of smart building technology and sustainability of high-rise buildings.
prerequisites: Must have completed all of ARCH1010 Structures/BLDG1002 Low-rise Construction and Land Surveying
antirequisites: Must not have completed CIVE3014

title: Construction Planning and Safety
overview: This course aims to equip students with foundational knowledge and practical skills in construction scheduling, enabling them to plan, organise, and control project timelines using both deterministic and stochastic methods. Students will develop the ability to analyse activities, allocate resources effectively, and anticipate potential delays to enhance efficiency and minimise risks in construction projects. This course further develops students’ understanding of construction safety legislation, risk management, and industry standards. This course enables students to assess hazards, investigate accidents, and apply effective control measures, while developing skills to promote ethical and legal responsibilities that prioritise worker wellbeing. Through applying safety alongside construction planning principles, students will be ready to manage projects confidently and responsibly in the dynamic construction industry.
learning_outcomes: Explain the principles of time management and their application in planning and scheduling construction projects.
Apply deterministic and stochastic scheduling techniques to develop, analyse, and control construction project timelines.
Analyse construction site hazards and causes of accidents.
Evaluate risk management strategies for construction sites to ensure compliance with WHS regulations and industry standards
Integrate safety management systems and practices into the preparation of safe work method statements
prerequisites: must have completed BLDG1000 Introduction to Construction Management
antirequisites: N/A

title: Building Services
overview: This course aims to equip students with essential knowledge and skills to understand and analyse building services such as mechanical, electrical, vertical transportation, fire safety, communication, and hydraulic systems. By examining the intricate dynamics of building services and considering their impacts on various aspects of construction and project management, students will develop critical thinking and problem-solving skills necessary for optimising total building performance and successful project management. This course aligns with the program's intent of preparing students for professional roles in the construction industry, equipping them with the knowledge and skills required for effective management of construction processes.
learning_outcomes: Explain the operational dynamics of building services, encompassing water, power, and drainage systems, and analyse the factors influencing their integration with public infrastructure
Analyse and optimise, using digital tools, building performance, (e.g., indoor lighting, acoustics, thermal comfort, and air quality), for occupants’ satisfaction and operational efficiency
Analyse the interactions between various building services
Explore the implications of building services on construction planning and project management, considering diverse project types and delivery methods
Identify key cost drivers in building service delivery and assess their impact on Total Building Performance, integrating cost-effective solutions
Discuss the interplay between building services management, building performance, and cost implications of services, and formulate strategies to achieve optimal building performance.
antirequisites: must not have completed CIVE2013 UO Building Services at the University of South Australia OR must not have completed CIVE2007 Building Services at the University of South Australia

title: Quantity Surveying Fundamentals and Cost Estimating
overview: This course aims to equip learners with fundamental knowledge and skills required for the practice of quantity surveying. The course introduces cost management principles and appropriate knowledge in respect to standard methods of measurement, measurement, bills of quantities, and principles of estimating cost of construction. The learners will develop analytical thinking and effective communication skills for quantity surveying practice. This course intends to introduce learners to the quantity surveying principles enabling them to continue other quantity surveying courses in the program.
learning_outcomes: Describe the role of Quantity Surveyors and cost management principles
Identify how a project scope is broken up into a series of construction trade packages
Demonstrate the ability to read and interpret construction documents
Demonstrate the ability to perform computerised measurement and pricing
Apply principles of standard measurement techniques for construction works
Apply estimating principles for construction works including tender preparation
antirequisites: N/A

title: Construction Contract Administration
overview: This course aims to equip learners with knowledge of the Australian legal system, the key principles of the law of contract and torts, the various forms of contract conditions used in the Australian construction industry, key construction contract administration concepts and terminology and subcontracting. Upon successful completion of the course, students will appreciate the significant role which law plays in the construction process and will have acquired the foundational legal knowledge necessary to understand key provisions in construction contracts and progress their further learning with respect to construction contract administration.
learning_outcomes: Describe how law is made, recorded, classified and administered in Australia
Recognise the differences and interactions between legislation, contract law, equity and law of torts in the context of the construction industry
Explain how to carry out an ethical tendering process for the appointment of a construction contractor and how construction contracts are formed
Demonstrate an understanding of construction contracts and their application to projects
Distinguish between the different types of subcontractors engaged on construction projects and how they are appointed
antirequisites: N/A

title: Infrastructure Construction
overview: This course aims to build an understanding of construction technology as applied to infrastructure projects including measurement and cost estimating of infrastructure work.
learning_outcomes: Understand the construction technologies applied to infrastructure projects
Understand the construction process of infrastructure projects
Propose cost plans of transport infrastructure projects based on measurement and estimating
Evaluate procurement methods and tendering strategies for infrastructure projects
prerequisites: must have completed all of ARCH1009 Construction Science and Materials/BLDG1002 Low-rise Construction and Land Surveying
antirequisites: N/A

title: Development Regulations and Building Codes
overview: This course aims to develop students’ understanding of planning and building regulations relevant to the construction industry. It covers the development approval process, as well as the key codes and standards that govern construction activities in Australia.
learning_outcomes: Relate the principles of development and control to various projects and localities
Review the Planning, Development and Infrastructure Act and Regulations and the related Australian standards
Relate the Building Code of Australia to construction projects using drawings and other information
Compose reports on building and planning matters and analyse non-compliance with regulations
antirequisites: Must not have completed BUIL4028

title: Risk, Quality and People Management
overview: Students will build a deeper understanding of the management of construction projects with a particular emphasis on risk, quality, and people management.
learning_outcomes: Apply risk management theory to identify, analyse and evaluate risks in construction projects
Recommend alternative courses of action to manage, monitor and control risks in construction projects
Apply quality management theory to prepare quality management plans for construction projects
Demonstrate business management skills including personnel and resources management, leadership, and communication in construction businesses
Demonstrate professionalism, teamwork and effective communication as a construction management professional
prerequisites: must have completed BLDG1000 Introduction to Construction Management
antirequisites: N/A

title: Commercial Management
overview: To provide students with essential knowledge and skills in relation to the commercial management of finance, working capital, cash flow, project costs, time-related prolongation costs, variations to contract scope, payment and final accounts on construction projects.
learning_outcomes: Generate financial viability reports, cash flow forecasts, cost reports and model working capital requirements with respect to construction projects
Evaluate prolongation costs arising from project delays, as well as the management of price fluctuations and cost escalation in construction projects.

Prepare and calculate interim progress payment claims, payment certificates/schedules, and final accounts on construction projects according to contractual requirements. Demonstrate an understanding of how post-contract variations to the scope of works are directed and valued according to contractual requirements.

Explain and demonstrate how the statutory payment and adjudication schemes in the building and construction industry security of payment legislation affect progress and final payments on construction projects
prerequisites: must have completed BLDG4007 Construction Contract Administration
antirequisites: N/A

title: Construction Management Research Methods
overview: This course is designed to cultivate a comprehensive understanding of research within the field of construction management. Students will be exposed to the fundamental nature of research and the processes involved in its execution. The course will explore the contemporary structure of research and familiarise students with various research methodologies, including quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-mode approaches. This course will guide students in utilising online resources and tools for efficient searching, identification, and retrieval of relevant research materials. This course also aims at introducing common data analysis techniques, enabling students to effectively process and interpret research findings. A critical component of the course focuses on fostering effective communication skills for research outcomes within the context of construction management. Students will be equipped to translate complex findings into impactful presentations and written reports specifically tailored for this audience. This course aligns with the program's intent to develop and apply research, communication, and professional skills.
learning_outcomes: Develop a comprehensive understanding of research fundamentals.
Develop an understanding of quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-mode research methodologies relevant to construction management.
Develop an understanding of appropriate data analysis techniques to interpret and draw meaningful conclusions from research findings.
Develop proficient communication skills to articulate research outcomes clearly and effectively
Develop skills in utilising online resources and tools proficiently to search, identify, retrieve, and critically evaluate relevant research materials
Develop a thorough understanding of key ethical considerations in research
antirequisites: Must not have completed CONMGNT_7008 Construction Research Methods at the University of Adelaide

title: Construction Management Professional Practice
overview: To utilise and apply learnings from academic study in a professional environment with structured guidance and assessment. The course prepares students for professional roles by enhancing their self-awareness and emphasising the importance of continuous professional and personal development. It formally recognises student engagement in industry experience required for future roles as qualified construction professionals.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the ability to identify and reflect on a range of skills and competencies needed to function as a professional in the construction industry.
Apply principles of construction management and program learning to real world solutions and evaluate results
Demonstrate capacity to contribute to and work within an organisation at a professional level, taking responsibility for delegated project tasks in an accountable and ethical way
Engage in independent, collaborative, and reflective learning towards building professional identity and develop and reflect on career goals
Demonstrate an understanding of the culture of the workplace, the construction industry and the relationship with other cultural backgrounds including their own
antirequisites: N/A
assessment: A range of assignments designed to support course outcomes – 10%

title: Construction Management Research Project A
overview: This course enables students to integrate knowledge gained throughout the Construction Management program, together with research skills developed in Research Methods, to design and develop a comprehensive research proposal. Building upon the fundamentals of scientific research, students will apply these skills to formulate a well-structured research design that addresses critical questions within the field of construction management. The course emphasises both independent and collaborative work, culminating in the submission of a written research proposal. This course will prepare students for Final Year Research Project B. The  Research Project courses prepare students for lifelong learning and the application of research as a  component of professional practice in construction management careers.
learning_outcomes: Consolidate theoretical and technical knowledge and research and analytical skills to plan and execute a research-based project
Apply Critical thinking skills to review published literature related to a research topic and synthesise a written literature review
Apply systems thinking to determine, develop and implement the most appropriate research method to investigate a research topic demonstrating a commitment to ethical actions
Demonstrate the ability to work as a member of a professional team, displaying both team-work skills and autonomy
prerequisites: must have completed BLDGX300 Construction Management Research Methods
antirequisites: N/A

title: Advanced Construction Management
overview: To develop advanced knowledge and applied skills in modern construction methods, business management, ethics, and professional practice for effective construction management. This course will assist students in obtaining knowledge and skills to apply modern construction methods and effectively manage construction-related businesses through strategic management, marketing, ethical practice, and professional management of business and industrial relations. It will improve students’ professionalism and leadership skills along with communication skills. This course aligns with the program’s intent of providing knowledge to commence professional practice in construction management discipline.
learning_outcomes: Compare and contrast differing organisational structures for construction-related organisations (including interstate and international companies) and explain how this affects their business decision making
Apply strategic management and marketing principles to support effective decision-making in the management of construction-related businesses.
Generate and evaluate key financial accounting data to make strategic business decisions and communicate outcomes with decision makers
Apply knowledge of the Australian industrial relations framework, professional practice and business ethics to the construction management profession
Analyse and evaluate modern construction methods and their application within the construction industry.
prerequisites: must have completed BLDG3002 Risk, Quality and People Management
antirequisites: N/A
assessment: A range of assignments designed to support course outcomes – 50%

title: Advanced Building Surveying
overview: Students will demonstrate an advanced understanding and apply principles of performance regulation, ethics and professional practice as a Building Surveyor.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the structure and operation of Local Governments, Statutory Authorities and private certifiers to the activities of the construction industry in Australia and in the international context
Discuss the professional services that building surveyors perform, addressing both the inspection/report and assessment-based work as well as the professional consulting role
Evaluate ethical courses of action, according to professional body ethical codes of conduct to be followed by building surveyors in various industry scenarios
Generate detailed building surveying related reports on buildings and carry out building inspections
prerequisites: must have completed BLDG3003 Building Surveying
antirequisites: must not have completed CIVE4045 UO Advanced Building Surveying at the University of South Australia OR must not have completed CIVE4032 Advanced Building Surveying at the University of South Australia

title: Advanced Quantity Surveying
overview: The course aims to provide students with advanced knowledge and skills of modern quantity surveying practices. Building upon concepts of quantity surveying practices introduced earlier, the course delves into life cycle costing, value management, tax depreciation, insurance assessments, and ethics for the quantity surveying profession. By understanding advanced quantity surveying practices, learners will develop critical thinking, analytical thinking, effective communication, teamwork skills and ethical practice essential for modern and professional quantity surveying practice. This course aligns with the program’s intent to excel learners to become leading professional quantity surveyors.
learning_outcomes: Synthesise knowledge in pre-contract quantity surveying services such as specialist procurement advice, value management processes, and tender evaluation & reporting.
Demonstrate intellectual interest, professional ethics and governance as a quantity surveying professional in a lifelong learning environment
Apply whole-of-life costing techniques for the choice of building materials and systems
Execute tax depreciation and insurance assessment in construction
Demonstrate professionalism, teamwork, and effective communication as a quantity surveying professional
prerequisites: must have completed BLDG3004 Cost Planning
antirequisites: N/A

title: Urban Design for Health and Sustainability
overview: Urban Design for Health and Sustainability course provides learners with an understanding of the interrelationship between urban design, public health, and sustainability, emphasising key principles and processes involved in urban design, with a specific focus on enhancing sustainability and public health. Through this course, learners will gain the knowledge and skills to critically evaluate various urban design strategies, examining their effectiveness in creating cities that are both environmentally sustainable and conducive to the well-being of their inhabitants. The course will also enable students to analyse real-world examples of successful urban planning practices, identifying key factors that contribute to the development of healthy, liveable, and resilient urban spaces. By combining theoretical insights with practical applications, the course prepares students to make informed decisions about urban design, empowering them to create urban environments that promote health, sustainability, and quality of life for diverse communities. Learning activities include case study analysis, tutorial exercises, and both collaborative and individual design-based assessments.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the key concepts link between urbanisation, urban design, public health and sustainability

Demonstrate a critical understanding of the urban design theories and principles along with analytical and practical approaches to create sustainable and healthy development in urban and regional context.
Apply urban design theoretical framework, concepts and guidelines to assess and develop healthier, more resilient and sustainable urban spaces at different scales and for different settings.
Perform a detailed appraisal of an urban development site/s using broader urban health and sustainability goals
antirequisites: N/A

title: Creative Worlds: Industries, Identities and Opportunities
overview: Students will be introduced to the Creative Arts, exploring frameworks to better understand the arts and cultural industries, and careers within these. Through case studies addressing the experiences of artists and cultural workers from a wide variety of cultural sectors, students will develop their own identities as creative professionals and pathways to creative work. By examining the nexus of artist, funding body, company, audience, government, economy and society, and critically reflecting on their own place within this nexus, students will gain important skills for project-planning, problem solving, and creative innovation.
learning_outcomes: Describe key theoretical and conceptual frameworks for understanding creative and cultural work.
Discuss the various stakeholders in creative fields, including audiences, industries, policy, critics, artists and platforms
Demonstrate knowledge of a chosen creative field and its opportunities.
Communicate effectively to translate their own creative ideas into project plans that can be used to propose relationships for collaboration.
Critically evaluate case studies of creative work to identify principles of effective creative processes as they relate to artistic production, projects and spaces.
antirequisites: N/A

title: Drawing for Art and Design
overview: This course will introduce students to fundamental skills and knowledge in drawing relevant to discipline specific contexts. Focussing on analogue drawing, students will learn to recognise and apply a range of materials and processes to generate ideas and develop design concepts and artworks.
learning_outcomes: Develop technical analogue skills using a range of mediums, materials and processes to create a range of drawings relevant to context, content and discipline
Apply systems of drawing and observation for representation and communication
Analyse and reflect upon visual content for discipline specific contexts
Apply drawing as a means of expression and exploration through visualisation, interpretation and observation
antirequisites: N/A

title: Introduction to Comicbooks as Literature
overview: This course will introduce students to the particular narrative strengths of the still-image, sequenced, visual format used in comic books and provide perspectives on the directions of comic books in Australia. The course will discuss the developing distinction between comics, graphic novels, graphic narratives and cartoons. In doing so it will trace the history of cartoons as the basis for the first comics to appear in Europe and North America, will examine the first popularisation of comic books into serialised format in the USA and the later split between fictional and non-fictional comics. In addition, this course will briefly trace the recent proliferation of comic books into cross-media forms such as the Super-Hero franchise films and the burgeoning genre of animated documentary films. This course will provide a basis for students to produce and interpret their own comic books, scripts and story boards for films and computer games.
antirequisites: must not have completed COMM1080 Introduction to Comicbooks as Literature at the University of South Australia

title: Creative Solutions: Reimagining Projects
overview: This interdisciplinary studio-based course presents opportunities for students to work together to solve real world problems for an industry partner. Students will develop their abilities to connect ideas and experience across specific creative disciplines, and to develop interdisciplinary knowledge and understanding. Working in teams, students will share responsibility and develop leadership capacities. The focus of projects includes a variety of crucial social challenges faced by arts and cultural community organisations, social enterprise; low carbon living and green industries; health and wellbeing; education; and creative enterprise development. This course culminates in a creative arts project showcase event.
learning_outcomes: Scope and undertake research relevant to a client focused project
Collaborate within cross-disciplinary and trans-disciplinary teams to create an output that meets clients’ objectives
Write up and present a rationale, approach, and final project proposal to relevant professional standard
Articulate how one’s own creative thinking and practice demonstrates the use of art to innovatively respond to social problems and enable the imagining of new futures
antirequisites: N/A

title: Artistic Work: Industries and the Creative Life
overview: This course uses the creation of graphic narratives as an example of a creative method through which to critically assess the relationships between artistic practice, life and industry. Students will study the history and practice of autobiographical art, covering a range of cultural perspectives, and will apply what they have learned by creating their own autobiographical graphic narratives. In so doing, this course facilitates students to interrogate the broader intersections between art as public good, sustaining their own creative work and the lives of other artists who grapple with these issues. This will enhance their understanding of their own creative aspirations and personal values, while also developing critical reflection and communication skills that will underlie their future strategic career decisions. In addition to working as thoughtful artists, this course prepares creative industry professionals to transfer their critical lens and skills to commercial arts and cultural organisations, political campaign management, arts and cultural management in local council, state and federal government agencies, education, communication media for private companies, or in the not-for-profit sector.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse works of art in terms of their formal properties, content and/or process of production.
Identify and discuss the way a work of art articulates with its historical and cultural context and evaluate its role and reception in society.
Articulate their subjective experience of relating to art work by communicating persuasively.
Develop, interpret and present their own works of art effectively to audiences.
antirequisites: N/A

title: Creative Arts Professional Experience
overview: In this course, students apply their understandings of potential pathways and career destinations through a Creative Arts Project centred on mentoring and networking experiences. Having researched potential pathways that are meaningful and relevant to their disciplinary interests, expertise and career aspirations, students will work on an approved project that will develop their career pathway. Drawing on their Creative Arts Project experience, students identify, reflect and report on their experience and how it informs their emerging career narrative.
learning_outcomes: Gain professional experience through an internship, project or other WIL experience in an industry relevant to their program.
Articulate and plan towards career goals, contextualising steps towards these within the professional experience activity. Develop skills in preparing a professional-standard resume and/or portfolio.

Demonstrate understandings of professionalism as it pertains to the discipline, and of connections between academic learning and professional practice, including application of networking skills in professionally focussed setting.
Apply the knowledge and skills acquired during their studies to undertake relevant professional tasks and produce effective outputs, and to reflect critically on this experience.
Explain and analyse the practice and role of a specific discipline within an organisation or industry, and reflect on the value of the WIL experience to ongoing learning in this area.
prerequisites: Must have completed at least 96 units of study
antirequisites: N/A
assumed_knowledge: Successful completion of all first and second year undergarduate core courses

title: Superheroes: Cinema and Comics
overview: One of the of the most popular forms of media of the early 21st century is inter-connected superhero films inspired by comic books. In this course, students will gain a deeper understanding of superhero films and comics and transmedia universes, as well as their historical influences, and the roles they have played in wider cultural debates about identity, power, ethics and society, using cutting edge digital tools to research these films and build important skills in data collection and analysis.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the cultural history of superhero media from a variety of perspectives.
Apply digital humanities methods to engage with creative texts through digital archives and algorithms.
Design and conduct a research project that investigates the textual and/or paratextual qualities of a set of cultural texts.
Demonstrate an understanding of the ways that comics can be used to communicate information by creating a short research comic.
antirequisites: N/A

title: Introduction to Illustration and Animation
overview: This course establishes the foundational practice-based knowledge and skills specific to illustration and animation. Students will be introduced to the studio environment where they will explore processes and principles of picture making specific to illustration and animation including composition, colour theory and application, selected animation principles and drawing processes and techniques for illustration and animation. Students will learn to recognise and apply discipline specific knowledge and skills in the execution of introductory level Illustration and Animation projects to provide a foundation for future development in illustration and animation practice.
learning_outcomes: Analyse pictorial content, context and structure
Apply foundational principles, elements and knowledge in the development of static and moving pictures
Demonstrate effective presentation methods and techniques relevant to illustration and animation contexts
Utilise digital and analogue mediums, techniques and processes for effective picture making and animation
Demonstrate an iterative and considered picture making process through reflective practice
Demonstrate representational drawing skills throughout the picture design process
antirequisites: N/A

title: Cinematic Design
overview: To introduce students to the practical and theoretical knowledge of Cinematic Design, and to develop student skills in the application of this knowledge for establishing the relationship between design principles and the process of designing for film, animation, and visual effects. Students will develop skills to identify, evaluate, construct, and apply key principles of cinematic design in contemporary screen production. Students will focus on the concept of ‘design language’, using metaphors of 'grammar' and 'vocabulary' taken from natural language that enrich the process of designing for film, animation, visual effects, and illustration, and apply these skills in practice using a variety of visual effects and computer graphics packages.
learning_outcomes: apply key concepts and principles in cinematic design
apply key concepts and principles in grammatical design
observe, analyse and adapt existing design languages to generate new creations
communicate ideas both visually and textually for cinematic media
work independently and collaboratively to ideate cinematic design concepts
antirequisites: N/A

title: Life Drawing
overview: This course aims to develop learners’ skills and knowledge to explore principles and practice of drawing the human figure and develop drawing accuracy and interpretive abilities. The course builds learners’ knowledge and skills in life drawing by fostering a variety of approaches to observing, analysing and drawing the human figure while reflecting on their own and others’ life drawing practice. Students in this course develop observational drawing, use a range of drawing mediums, and employ conceptual and technical processes relevant to the field.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate drawing and observational skills to develop coherent, original drawn forms of the human figure for representation and communication.
Apply various drawing techniques to develop original drawings of the human figure.
Utilise a variety of mediums, and conceptual and technical processes to produce a range of figurative drawings.
Apply critical reflection and academic referencing skills to analyse representations of the figurative and articulate student’s own drawing practice.
prerequisites: must have completed GRAP1001 Drawing for Art and Design
antirequisites: N/A

title: The Art of Collecting: Creativity, Collections and Cultural Connections
overview: Culture and creativity are built through collecting and connecting ideas, objects, people and experiences across time and space. Throughout human history we have collected – from family heirlooms, to works of art, to scientific specimens. This course explores the complex history of collecting using case studies from South Australia and around the globe. This course will explore how, what and why humans collect. How have the collections of key cultural institutions come into being and what biases were at play in their development? Using “The Art of Collecting” as a broad conceptual lens to think through the way cultural institutions such as museums, galleries, libraries and archives students will examine how meaning is derived from the ways that different objects are brought together, combined, or excluded. The Art of Collecting questions how we can use collections today to tell stories of the past, to create meaning, and to inspire new narratives and cultural works.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate the history, and politics of collecting and the ongoing impact of these legacies for cultural institutions and communities.
Show an understanding of how objects move into, through and out of cultural institutions.
Think critically about the ways in which the GLAM sector uses collections to tell stories about the past, present and future.
Show an understanding of the legacy of collecting including the contemporary ethical, practical and environmental considerations.
antirequisites: N/A

title: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Art
overview: The course explores the vast diversity of historical and contemporary Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander art. Using case studies, and prioritising First Nations voices, we explore the extraordinary depth of art practice represented across Australia. From some of the worlds earliest rock art, to Arnhem Land bark paintings, Hermannsburg watercolours, and cutting-edge contemporary artist collectives in Sydney and Melbourne, this course offers unique insights into the lives, cultural influences, and impact of Aboriginal artists and their communities. This course draws heavily on the internationally significant art collections within local cultural institutions and gives a behind-the-scenes look into the management of Aboriginal art collections. Key anthropological, ethnographic and museological issues arising from the collecting and display of Aboriginal art and objects in museums and galleries are also discussed.
learning_outcomes: Recognise the diversity of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander histories, cultures and creative practices, and identify the major styles and concerns of key movements and artists.
Understand the historical, political, economic and ethical features of the production, consumption and reception of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander art.
Understand and critique the scholarly, institutional and public discourses concerning Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander art.
Critically reflect on the contributions of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander artists to Australian cultural, social, and political life and to art globally.
antirequisites: N/A

title: Creative Labour
overview: This course draws upon various perspectives from within creative arts, communication, cultural and media studies, sociology, and internet studies to explore the changing nature of creative labour. This course explores scholarly debates about work in the cultural and creative industries. Through studying theoretical and historical perspectives and empirical examples from research into work in the contemporary media and creative industries, students will consider how creative work is being imagined, understood, structured, and represented as a particular kind of work, and consider the importance of portfolio careers and networking to creative labour. Students will learn to interrogate the way the nature of work in this sector typically leads to a lack of social inclusion and diversity.
learning_outcomes: Outline research and critical debate about working practices in the cultural and creative industries
To analyse, using relevant theoretical ideas, scenarios of creative work
Identify a diverse range of working practices and evaluate how these impact on career pathways
Analyse how the pathways into creative work impact the demographics of creative labour and be aware of relevant corrective interventions
Recognise the impact of public and private funding contexts on work in the creative industries
Critically reflect on the application of professional practices in the context of a creative career, including the impact of AI on creative work
prerequisites: must have completed CREA1000 Creative Worlds: Industries, Identities and Opportunities
antirequisites: N/A

title: Curation, Performance and Exhibition
overview: In this course students will work in teams to build real-world exhibitions or curate a hypothetical festival. They will explore the art and practices integral to developing vibrate creative industries, focusing on curation, performance and exhibition. Students' projects will be informed by recent scholarship and conceptual thinking regarding audiences, industries and future technologies. Their learning will be supported by guest lectures from galleries, libraries and museums (GLAM), and other cultural sectors.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a knowledge of the curatorial processes that support festivals and exhibition events
Apply management skills in practice required for an event, including planning and development
Prepare and deliver curated event documentation, such as a program guide for an event, or catalogue for an exhibition
Apply effective communication strategies with key stakeholders for successful festival planning and logistics
prerequisites: must have completed CREA1000 Creative Worlds: Industries, Identities and Opportunities
antirequisites: N/A

title: Digital Heritage
overview: Digital heritage augments, transforms, preserves and communicates the cultural significance and value of real-world heritage. Despite impressive recent advances and increasingly accessible software and hardware, the digital heritage field faces critical challenges. For example, digital heritage experts have noted even large and expensive projects can suddenly vanish or become inoperable and obsolete; a phenomenon they termed the vanishing virtual. In this course, the advances and challenges of the digital (virtual, interactive, mobile, wearable and immersive technologies) applied to cultural heritage are reviewed, in Australia and internationally. Students will explore recent trends in digital collections, digital media, and digital archives; creative AI; extended reality (AR, MR, VR; cyberculture, virtual worlds, and the metaverse.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate and respond to challenges facing the Australian heritage sector
Analyse the place of First Nations communities and the challenges and opportunities of applying digital technology to help support preserve and communicate their storytelling and values systems
Demonstrate a nuanced understanding of the advances and challenges of digital heritage in Australian and globally
Identify and critically analyse scholarship relating to digital heritage, its impact, usefulness, and relation to current social and environmental challenges
Think critically through speculative design about the ways in which digital heritage can encapsulate, augment, or threaten traditional methods to preserve and disseminate the past
Use their creative strengths and skills to transmit digital solutions to current challenges facing the GLAM sector
prerequisites: must have completed CREA1000 Creative Worlds: Industries, Identities and Opportunities
antirequisites: N/A

title: Digital Project Management
overview: This course equips students with essential project management and career development skills applicable across the interactive media and software development industries. Students will explore relevant theories and tools utilised in these fields such as agile/scrum and will have the opportunity to apply this knowledge in practical contexts.
learning_outcomes: Create and maintain comprehensive project roadmaps and development plans using Agile/Scrum methodologies and workflows.
Apply theoretical knowledge and practical skills in project planning and execution in ways that are responsive to industry demands.
Execute project tasks and adjust project plans based on feedback and changing requirements during the lifecycle of real-world project.
Analyse project outcomes using critical reflection and root cause analysis techniques to adapt processes and practice for continued improvement
antirequisites: N/A

title: Web Design Principles
overview: This course introduces students to foundational concepts and practical skills in web design, covering the history and evolution of the web, essential visual design principles, and core technologies such as HTML, CSS, responsive design and coding libraries. Students will learn to source and edit digital assets, ensure web accessibility, and gain an introduction to Content Management Systems, preparing them to create visually appealing and accessible websites.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the history and evolution of the web by examining key developments and their impact on society, demonstrating an understanding of how past innovations influence modern web technologies
Develop functional skills in using HTML and CSS, responsive design frameworks and code libraries, through developing responsive and interactive elements
Apply basic web design visual and accessibility principles to create aesthetically pleasing and accessible user-friendly web pages
Demonstrate basic skills in content management systems, to build and manage a basic website
antirequisites: N/A
assessment: Interactive Questions, Interactive Questions, Interactive Questions – 15%

title: Web Development
overview: Through specialised study and practical engagement, students develop skills in interpreting design briefs, producing web preproduction materials, and communicating and pitching design concepts to stakeholders. They gain expertise in web infrastructure management; in building and managing functional websites using content management systems; and in implementing and evaluating accessibility standards to ensure compliant and user-friendly websites.
learning_outcomes: Develop functional website preproduction materials from design briefs and effectively communicate and pitch web design concepts to stakeholders.
Apply web infrastructure management skills, including domain registration, hosting setup, and implementing security measures, to maintain reliable websites.
Effectively utilise content management systems (CMS) to build and manage functional websites to meet client goals, including customising themes and templates, ensuring ethical use of digital assets.
Implement and evaluate accessibility standards to meet industry expectations for compliant and user-friendly websites.
prerequisites: must have completed MDIA2001 Web Design Principles
antirequisites: N/A

title: Digital Mediascapes
overview: Digital Mediascapes expands student understanding of media production by considering how aspects of digital media intersect with local and global issues of space, aesthetics, personal, political, cultural and public life. Drawing on interdisciplinary studies, students will experiment with the affordances of digital media to explore the potential for new types of screen-based narratives.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an advanced knowledge of the continuities and the differences between traditional screen media and contemporary digital media formats
Critically analyse how digital technologies have altered the social, cultural and political potential of narrative media
Apply advanced theoretical and practical approaches to digital storytelling
Work in teams to produce transmedia storytelling plans and content
antirequisites: N/A

title: Web Design Portfolio
overview: This course prepares final-year students for professional careers in web design by engaging them in real-world client projects within the Adelaide University Web Design Studio . Students will work in small teams to interpret client briefs, develop proposals, and deliver professional presentations for real-world clients. They will apply industry-standard tools and project management practices to deliver complete websites on schedule, create detailed handover documentation, and critically reflect on their professional development, teamwork experiences, and potential career pathways in web design.
learning_outcomes: Collaborate in small teams to interpret real-world client briefs, develop proposals, and deliver professional client presentations.
Apply industry-standard tools and project management techniques to deliver complete client websites within specified timeframes as part of a collaborative team.
Create comprehensive handover documentation to ensure successful client project completion.
Reflect critically on professional development, team collaboration experiences, and career opportunities in web design.
prerequisites: must have completed MDIA3001 Web Development
antirequisites: N/A

title: Introduction to Festivals
overview: This course will introduce students to the study of festivals, including the histories and cultures of a variety of festival types. Students will attend festival performances and be introduced to key conceptual frameworks for understanding festivals, including social and cultural capital, and the broad categories of festival types, such as open access and curated festivals. Reflecting on case studies of well-known festivals, students will develop an understanding of the relationship between festivals and audiences and the impact of arts and cultural festivals locally, nationally and internationally.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the history and development of festivals and their connection to place and culture.
Articulates the relationship between festivals and the public sphere.
Describe the history, roles, impacts of arts/cultural festivals locally, nationally and internationally.
Describe the various career pathways within arts/cultural festivals and reflect on how these relate to their own graduate career aspirations.
antirequisites: N/A

title: Creative Tourism: Food, Wine and Festivals
overview: To facilitate students understanding of food, wine and festivals as a special interest tourism by exploring various emerging issues and business practices in the context of creative tourism entrepreneurship.
learning_outcomes: Discuss and assess the ways in which the tourism industry uses food, wine, drinks, and festivals as nuclei for special interest tourism (including creative tourism) locally and internationally.
Critique multiple contexts and theories of festivals, food and wine tourism from the creative industry perspective.
Analyse the emerging characteristics of tourist markets, products and services offered by food, wine and festival industries.
Propose new food, wine and festival enterprise opportunities in the context of creative tourism.
antirequisites: N/A

title: The Adelaide Festival Experience
overview: In this course students investigate the Adelaide Festival and its place in the broader arts ecology. Through attending key festivals and events, students will gain basic literacy in theatrical genres, directing styles and reviewing. Students will explore debates around literary festivals, censorship and free speech, the nature of the festival experience, and the ethical and ecological responsibilities of modern festivals. In this course students all attend the same productions at the Adelaide Festival and Adelaide Writers Week, to build on their knowledge of how curation, sponsorship and festival-added experiences inform the sector.
learning_outcomes: Describe and evaluate key features of a theatrical work of art using appropriate discipline specific language
Analyse theatrical productions in relation to conventions of theatrical staging and technique, traditions of performance and content
Identify and analyse models of creativity, collaboration and curation in relation to the Adelaide Festival
Discuss the history of the Adelaide Festival, evaluate its relationship to place and community, and analyse debates about measuring the Festival’s value
Analyse the role of arts festivals in society in relation to debates about inclusion and accessibility, free speech and ethical funding
Analyse critically the Adelaide Festival’s relation to the local arts ecology
antirequisites: N/A

title: Festivals Operations Management
overview: This course focuses on the fundamental managerial knowledge and skills which festival managers are expected to master as well as addressing current socio-political and economic challenges influencing the industry. The course examines all areas necessary for the successful delivery of festivals including the financial planning required to realise the program, legal requirements especially those relating to charitable status, relationships with key stakeholders and funders, fundraising, operational management and strategic development and marketing. Successful festival delivery is dependent on rigorous and well-planned operations management as a backbone.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the operation and administrative systems that support festivals.
Critically analyse contemporary issues in festival operations, applying research skills to identify and address key challenges in festival management.
Evaluate real-life festivals using festival management theories to solve operational issues and ensure long-term financial sustainability.
Apply knowledge of festival management, including program design, budgeting, funding strategies, and delivery planning, to propose a comprehensive festival plan.
Effectively communicate and justify festival management and execution strategies to stakeholders, ensuring alignment with the festival’s goals.
prerequisites: must have completed HOSP1001 Foundations of Event Management
antirequisites: N/A

title: Introduction to Games Design
overview: This course will provide students with a foundation in the key aspects of design and production for games, including the tools and theories of the games production industry. Students will develop an understanding of the history of games and the role of the game designer. They will explore game design theory and apply this to the design of their own game. Students will work through the game design process from initial game ideation through game design pre-production and the development of a completed game prototype and initial game play testing.
learning_outcomes: Examine and analyse games utilising game design theory and frameworks
Apply introductory skills to develop game design pre-production artefacts
Use introductory skills to ideate and realise game design prototypes
Apply the essential communication and collaboration skills required in the games production industry
Develop an understanding of User Experience and Interface Design in games.
antirequisites: must not have completed GRAP1030 Introduction to Games Design at the University of South Australia

title: Visual Asset Design for Games
overview: Equip students with the skills to design and create visually appealing graphical assets, both practical and efficient for game design. Students will learn to create 3D models suitable for game environments, generate assets with optimal poly counts, enhance models using advanced aesthetic techniques, and design and map 2D textures to 3D models. Students will compose an industry ready portfolio showcasing their modelling abilities.
learning_outcomes: Create refined 3D meshes, ready for renderer.
Produce visually appealing and technically sound game assets.
Design, construct and map 2D textures to 3D models.
Develop an industry relevant portfolio to showcase output professionally.
antirequisites: N/A

title: Immersive Media Design and Development 1
overview: VR (Virtual Reality), MR (Mixed Reality) and AR (Augmented Reality) are technologies that are quickly changing the way we consume media, play games, educate, and communicate. In this course students will learn key skills associated with designing and developing software for these platforms and will experience these technologies through hands-on play. Putting emphasis on production workflow and effective design, students will learn how to create digital assets for XR systems (3D models, textures/materials, sounds), as well as learn how to import these assets and apply interactivity in game engine.
learning_outcomes: Build digital assets (such as 3D models, textures/materials, and sounds) specific for XR platforms
Identify and implement appropriate design methodologies for immersive technology development, especially from a physiological perspective
Apply foundational literacy in game engine use, asset management and development pipelines
Effectively design an immersive XR experience
antirequisites: N/A

title: Game Environment Design
overview: This course will provide students with the knowledge and skills to design games to suit an identified audience.
