Communicate complex ideas, analyses and findings appropriately, persuasively and succinctly to diverse audiences.
antirequisites: N/A

title: Creativity and Innovation
overview: This course aims to uplift students’ creativity knowledge and practical skills to develop and manage innovative solutions to complex issues identified in the modern workplace and for societies in general. The course will do more than reinforcing the vague notions of innovation and creativity as buzzwords but will provide students a practical toolkit to create and exploit innovation opportunities in organisations via project-based tasks.
learning_outcomes: Apply tools and techniques to generate creative and innovative opportunities that are actionable, ethical and sustainable.
Critically analyse creative leadership, innovation culture and organisational settings that enhance collaborative creativity and innovation development
Demonstrate advanced level communication within a collaborative team that fosters innovation development.
Developing innovative propositions to solve social-economic challenges using co-creative processes and individual creative roles.
antirequisites: N/A

title: Design Thinking
overview: This course develops advanced capability in Design Thinking as both a methodology and a mindset for innovation in complex, uncertain environments. Students will critically engage with the full cycle of human-centred design while also examining the broader dimensions that shape its practice, including ethics, sustainability, stewardship, and leadership. By integrating systems thinking, reflective practice, and creative experimentation, the course challenges students to reframe problems, generate transformative solutions, and apply altered ways of thinking that are responsive to societal change and responsible innovation.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate the interdisciplinary theories, frameworks, and global perspectives that underpin Design Thinking, and apply them to complex organisational challenges.
Employ advanced communication and collaboration skills to effectively engage with multiple stakeholders and demonstrate leadership within Design Thinking processes.
Apply human-centred design principles (empathy, define, ideate, prototype, test) and complementary frameworks to design, develop, and test innovative, ethical, and sustainable solutions.
Integrate digital tools, systems thinking, and technological approaches into Design Thinking practice to solve complex management and innovation problems.
Critically reflect on personal and professional growth as an innovation leader, demonstrating commitment to stewardship, cultural diversity, and lifelong learning.
antirequisites: N/A
assessment: Data Collection and/or Analysis, Performance, Peer Review – 50%

title: Managing Tourism and Hospitality Operations
overview: The course aims to prepare students for managerial careers within the tourism and hospitality sectors, focusing on the management of business operations through the lens of key departments including marketing, finance, HRM, risk, and logistics. It is designed to develop students’ working knowledge of the industry and the operating tasks involved in managing tourism and hospitality businesses.
learning_outcomes: Explain the role and key operational functions of tourism and hospitality organisations, and challenges and demands facing managers
Analyse the performance of key operations in tourism and hospitality firms - including risk, logistics, marketing, and HR
Develop and interpret key financial statements and performance indicators to support managerial decision making for tourism and hospitality firms
Analyse internal and external factors in order to make evidence based managerial decisions
Discuss how sustainability practices in tourism and hospitality firms affect the triple bottom line of profit, people and environment
antirequisites: N/A

title: Tourism, Event and Hospitality Practicum
overview: Projects are negotiated between the School and the sponsor within the host organisation, and may include a marketing plan, social and economic development plans, research, business development, customer relations, events management, or any other negotiated project. As well as undertaking an agreed project, students will be involved in observations, meetings, clerical work and administration, to gain deeper insights into the day-to-day functioning of the business.
learning_outcomes: Plan, coordinate and undertake a range of professional activities and engage in reflective practices to facilitate personal and professional growth
Identify skills and capabilities that intersect effectively with the needs of industry
Apply and practice good communication skills in a variety of professional and/or cultural contexts
Evaluate the internship experience in relation to personal career goals
antirequisites: N/A

title: Marketing for Tourism, Events and Hospitality
overview: The aim of this course is to allow students to gain and apply knowledge in the area of experiential tourism and marketing. The course will enable students to analyse travel behaviour, identify market opportunities to design an innovative experiential product, and propose a bespoke marketing strategy. The course will emphasise links with other courses in program through case studies of effective marketing strategies for tourism, events, and hospitality. The course content and assessment will foster graduate qualities such as problem-solving and communication skills and ability to propose innovative and sustainable solutions for the industry.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate opportunities for existing and new experiential travel, events, and hospitality products based on research of global and local market trends
Critically analyse travel motivations and behaviour to identify viable target markets
Propose a creative experiential product that responds to identified market opportunities and travel needs
Devise an appropriate marketing strategy for the implementation of a proposed product
Apply relevant theories to idea generation and implementation strategy
Communicate devised strategies in a variety of formats, as appropriate for industry and academic audiences
antirequisites: N/A

title: Managing Venues and EventScapes
overview: This course develops students’ understanding of the link between the physical environment and event outcomes for a range of stakeholders including businesses and consumers. Applying concepts from psychology and marketing, and using an environmental management lens, students evaluate how event experiences are shaped by physical settings within a range of spatial scales. The course emphasises the creation of diversity in cultural venues and the role of venues in urban development.
learning_outcomes: Apply concepts from psychology, marketing, and environmental management to critically analyse how physical environments influence event experiences and diversity in cultural venues

Critically evaluate the role of servicescape in shaping service quality perceptions and stakeholder relationships across different spatial scales and propose innovative opportunities that demonstrate an understanding of how these attributes impact organisational performance outcomes
Critically assess the use of design as a communication strategy in event and venue contexts
Evaluate the role of venues in urban development and their contribution to cultural and economic outcomes
antirequisites: N/A

title: Event Leveraging and Legacy
overview: The course aims to equip students with the knowledge and skills for strategic event management, optimising the benefits of hosting events through event legacy and leveraging. By expanding upon foundational concepts of event management, the course explores the enduring benefits of event legacies and strategies to utilise events as catalysts for positive changes. Designed to enhance critical thinking and analysis skills crucial for strategic use of events, the course prepares students to excel in any field related to event management or involvement.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the diverse event legacies on host societies
Recommend approaches to enhance legacies for a broader range of communities and individuals
Propose event leveraging activities to maximise the benefits of hosting events
Develop strategies to achieve successful and sustainable event outcomes
antirequisites: N/A

title: Digital Innovations in Tourism, Events and Hospitality
overview: Information has been described as the lifeblood of tourism, with information and communication technologies (ICT) playing a key role in tourism management and operations. With digital innovations driving and fostering radical change in the sector, enabling firms to streamline operations, increase productivity, enrich customer service and enhance competitiveness, understanding how to leverage and manage technology-based innovations has become a critical issue. Adopting a management, as opposed to a technical, approach, this course aims to develop your management skills and competencies in exploiting information and computer technologies within the broad tourism sector, as well as anticipating their revolutionary impacts on three major tourism stakeholders: tourism demand; tourism suppliers; and tourism destinations.
learning_outcomes: Explain the transformative impact of digital developments on customers, organisations, and destinations within tourism, hospitality and events.
Interpret the role of digital in enriching tourism experiences, enhancing business operations, and developing new tourism offerings.
Demonstrate the ability to use managerial skills to exploit digital to improve the performance and competitiveness of tourism firms and destinations.
Demonstrate critical analytical skills in predicting and managing technological change and innovation in tourism.
antirequisites: N/A

title: Sustainable Destination Management
overview: This course actively discusses and analyses various debates over sustainable destination management of tourism impacts to gain critical insights into this well sought-after topic. Specific attention is given to numerous efforts to achieve sustainability goals, considering place, people, culture, local economy, and environment. Strategies across social, cultural, political, economic, and environmental aspects, and implications from government, business/industry and local stakeholders are discussed. The course prepares students to enhance their critical and reflective thinking skills on debating concepts and case studies as well as their creativity to tackle the complex set of tourism impacts for tourist destinations to be more sustainable.
learning_outcomes: Argue a case for and against the proposition that tourism has the capacity to promote sustainable development goals
Critique different levels of economic costs and benefits of tourism on international business and tourism destinations
Assess theoretical concepts and tools to manage various impacts of tourism on destination resources, culture and society
Develop effective strategies for minimising negative impacts of tourism and for sustainable tourism development
antirequisites: N/A

title: Planning Law
overview: Learners develop an understanding of legal principles informing property rights including land rights and Native Title and legal principles and procedures underpinning state based land use policy, regulatory functions and legislative obligations/frameworks in professional practice.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the legal basis of Torrens title system and aboriginal land rights
Analyse the legal context of urban and regional development and its relevance to real-world scenarios
Critically review planning law on strategy planning, plan review and implementation
Examine legislative instruments governing zoning, property rights and dispute resolution
prerequisites: must have completed all of ARCHX302 Planning Governance, Stakeholders, Politics and Policy/ARCHX303 Theory and Practice in Urban and Regional Planning
antirequisites: N/A

title: Development Assessment
overview: The aim of this course is to equip learners with the skills and knowledge to conduct and write development assessment reports within the planning regulatory system in South Australia and be able to adapt that learning to other national and international jurisdictions. The course delves into logic of development assessment steps and the procedures for determining a proposed development’s suitability in terms of endorsed policy outcomes and the public interest. This includes awareness of the parameters and discretion to achieve good development outcomes based on merit. Learners will develop confidence in negotiating the development assessment process as a regulator and as the advocate of a development proponent. This course aligns with the program's intent to provide a comprehensive understanding of professional development assessment practice that promotes sustainable development.
learning_outcomes: Understand and interpret current land use planning policies, instruments and development assessment procedures
Analyse development applications and make recommendations
Prepare development assessment reports
Understand land use policy amendment procedures and prepare policy amendment reports
prerequisites: Must have completed all of ARCHX302 Planning Governance, Stakeholders, Politics and Policy/ARCHX303 Theory and Practice in Urban and Regional Planning
antirequisites: N/A

title: Social Planning and Community Issues
overview: The aim of this course is to provide students with theories, evidence, concepts and skills that can be used to establish goals and strategies in supporting individual and community well being in existing neighbourhoods or proposed residential developments, framed by relevant land use planning, development assessment or other statutory processes. As such the concepts and skills could be considered to be helping to mediate the pace and scale of urbanisation, commonly referred to as growth management, and to help address emerging threats to wellbeing associated with economic and other issues. In this course social planning as a set of tools and values is understood to be either mandatory or voluntary under the following circumstance when: • identifying and reporting the intended and unintended social impacts of land use/development policy and decisions • determining current and anticipated human service and social infrastructure facilities for an existing community and or geographical area and preparing an implementation plan • developing plans for specific population groups at a given area - e.g. people with disabilities, older people, adolescents • undertaking master planning for proposed communities
learning_outcomes: Apply contemporary social theory to the social stratification dynamics in Australian society
Analyse social issues and social trends in the context of patterns of urbanisation in Australian
Critique social plans and social policy formation at national, state and local levels
Utilise indicators such as those of community disadvantage and community strength to underpin local level social planning
prerequisites: must have completed ARCHX302 Planning Governance, Stakeholders, Politics and Policy
antirequisites: N/A

title: Research Methods in Planning
overview: To develop an advanced understanding of how to conceive a research project with a clear rationale, apply diverse research methodologies, and exercise critical judgement in the context of urban and regional planning. This course equips learners with the knowledge and skills necessary to conduct research pertinent to urban and regional planning. It introduces a variety of methodological approaches and theoretical frameworks for designing planning research, encompassing both formal scientific models and practice-based approaches. Learners will engage in conducting a relevant literature review, formulating research questions, and identifying and justifying an appropriate research design that considers a broad spectrum of methodological options. The course aligns with the program’s objective of developing planning principles and research skills to investigate and address the dynamic relationship between society and space through qualitative and quantitative research.
learning_outcomes: Conduct literature review and identify existing knowledge gaps to inform new research direction, themes and/or theoretical conceptualisation.
Develop research aim/s and key questions to guide the research project, considering scope and limitations.
Select an appropriate research methodology and method and explore the applications and limitations
Explore ethical research in planning research projects, including respectful and culturally responsive engagement with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples and Country
Communicate a research proposal using academic language that includes the framework for a Planning Research Project.
antirequisites: N/A

title: Urban Design and Master Planning Studio
overview: This course aims to equip learners with the knowledge and skills to address a client’s proposed development through the application of advanced urban design and master planning skills. The course addresses all components of the process of client engagement from brief interpretation, site analysis, design proposal through costing and master planning sequencing. By practicing professional engagement skills for urban design, learners will develop critical thinking and problem-solving skills essential for creating visionary strategies and design proposals. This course aligns with the program's intent to prepare learners for the challenges inherent in meeting the highest industry expectations of urban designers in pursuit of sustainable development.
learning_outcomes: Understand and apply urban design processes, from concept to capital work execution, by developing a master plan for a given site from an urban or regional area
Work collaboratively with a client to determine when and what sustainable urban design interventions might be appropriate for a given site
Integrate sustainable urban design theoretical framework and practical applications to address urban and regional development issues
Utilise specialised software to analyse, design and manage urban environments
Critically evaluate the effectiveness of design interventions, considering how they will be implemented, by whom, and within what timeframe
prerequisites: must have completed ARCHX304 Urban Design for Health and Sustainability
antirequisites: N/A

title: Research Project in Planning
overview: This course provides students with the opportunity to independently design and complete a research project in the field of urban and regional planning. Students will formulate a research question, undertake a critical literature review, design an appropriate methodology, gather and analyse data, and present their findings. Guided by a supervisor, students will demonstrate advanced skills in ethical research practice, analytical reasoning, and professional communication. The course culminates in a 9,000-word research project and is a capstone experience that supports pathways into planning practice or further research.
learning_outcomes: Identify and refine a research topic, design a feasible research project, and formulate clear research questions addressing a relevant issue in urban and regional planning.
Apply ethical and rigorous research methods to collect, analyse and interpret primary and/or secondary data to address the research question
Demonstrate research independence, self-direction, effective time management, good communication, and responsiveness to critical feedback
Produce and present an independent research project that articulates a coherent argument, draws evidence-based conclusions, and contributes to the advancement of planning theory, policy, or practice
prerequisites: must have completed ARCH6304 Research Methods in Planning
antirequisites: N/A

title: Urban Planning Professional Experience
overview: This course provides urban planning learners with specialised practical expertise to apply to their discipline knowledge and skills within a work integrated learning environment, to compile the outcomes of that experience as a professional and transferable product, and critically reflect upon their experience.
learning_outcomes: Gain professional experience in an industry, organisation or project relevant to the discipline of urban planning.
Perform selected tasks, including the use of applications, at an advanced level consistent within urban planning practice in a professional setting
Demonstrate increased understanding of the social and ethical role of the urban planning professional in practice
Communicate with increasing confidence and efficacy in a professional setting
antirequisites: N/A

title: Advanced Study Tour
overview: Students will undertake a supervised study tour to explore the social, cultural, historical, political, economic and other relevant characteristics of the location visited, and identify issues related to their discipline area in historical and contemporary contexts. The nature of the content will vary according to the disciplinary mix of participating students and the specific characteristics of the location. Projects and assessments for the Study Tour will extend students' knowledge within a regional, national or international context. The study tour, when scheduled, will be open to students of selected programs.
learning_outcomes: Articulate cultural aspects and contexts in the discipline area
Identify issues which influence practices and outcomes in local and global contexts through direct experience in the study tour
Synthesise and communicate knowledge gained through coherent documentation
antirequisites: N/A

title: Sensory Studies
overview: This course involves teaching sessions that may be attended by both Undergraduate and Postgraduate students. This course provides a scientifically based introduction to sensory evaluation and its relationship to the winemaking process, and promotes the development of technically accurate wine assessment skills. The physiology of taste receptors, olfaction and the structure of oral mucosa are examined. Recent advances in knowledge, including the function of signal transduction molecules and protein structure are used to explain current models of flavour, astringency and taste perception. Basic flavour chemistry of grapes and wine is introduced. An introduction to sensory measurement theory, psychophysics, aroma and taste interactions, threshold measurement, and the psychological and physiological factors affecting perception is presented. The concept of adaptation and its application to the sensory evaluation of wines, and elements of good sensory practice including data collection and statistical analysis are described. The practical program will be used to develop basic skills in sensory assessment of wines leading to the interpretation of wine characteristics in terms of wine style and quality. This is achieved by a progressive development of sensory skills, using model solutions to depict basic tastes and their interaction, followed by a detailed examination of white and red table, fortified and sparkling wines.
learning_outcomes: Recognise the basic tastes and tactile sensations and describe their interactions and the mechanisms of how we perceive them.
Explain the principles of sensory physiology and psychology upon which sensory assessment is based and appreciate the factors that affect perception.
Describe the principles and practices of sensory measurement and quality assessment.
Draw sound conclusions and make recommendations following appropriate sensory experimentation and statistical analysis.
Explain the concept of sensory thresholds.
Have knowledge of the compounds responsible for wine aroma and flavour.
Identify common wine faults, their sensory characteristics and explain their origins.
Define wine characteristics in terms of grape variety, wine style, aging potential and quality.
Communicate confidently and succinctly their perceptions of wine to others using technically correct terminology
Further develop organisational and written and verbal presentation skills.
antirequisites: must not have completed OENOLOGY7019WT Sensory Studies at the University of Adelaide

title: Introductory Winemaking
overview: The course provides an introduction to modern wine production through the perspective of the Australian wine industry. Introductory topics in grape and wine chemistry are described, including acidity and the impacts of grape and wine acids in winemaking, sulphur dioxide and its uses in winemaking, phenolic compounds and their role in wine composition, and the effects of oxidation upon wine during maturation. All aspects of wine production including harvest, fruit processing, white and red vinification techniques, and alcoholic and malolactic fermentation are described. The principles and practice of processes to stabilise and clarify juices and wines are introduced. Practical activities during the course include an introduction to the techniques of basic chemical and microbiological analysis of grape juice, fermenting musts and final wines, management of a small-scale fermentation under defined conditions, and a visit to a commercial winery.
learning_outcomes: Describe the effects of acids and acidity on grape and wine composition and on the control of the winemaking process.
Explain how sulfur dioxide management is used in winemaking.
Explain the role and management of phenolic compounds during winemaking processes.
Describe the basic operations of grape harvesting and processing.
Describe the unit processes and equipment used in fermentation, pressing and post-fermentation treatments and their impacts on the final wine style outcomes.
Explain how different styles of white and red table wine are produced.
Describe the effects of aging, maturation and oxidation on wine composition.
Explain the basic principles of the management of yeast during the alcoholic fermentation and of bacterial cultures during the secondary fermentation.

Demonstrate familiarity and competence with the practical skills and techniques used in grape and wine chemical analysis. This will include the planning and reporting of analyses, the use of apparatus to measure pH, titratable acidity, sulfur dioxide, volatile acidity and alcohol, plus the use of spectrophotometric measurements for wine phenolics
Demonstrate an understanding of the conduct of an alcoholic fermentation and of the planning required to undertake practical winemaking operations.
prerequisites: Must have completed CHEM1002 Chemistry 1A OR must have completed CHEM1003 Chemistry 1B AND must have completed BUSI5028 Foundations of Wine Science
antirequisites: Must not have completed OENOLOGY7028WT Introductory Winemaking at the University of Adelaide
assessment: Short Response Questions, Short Response Questions – 10%

title: Viticultural Methods and Procedures
overview: This course involves teaching sessions that may be attended by both Undergraduate and Postgraduate students. This course looks at the practices associated with the development and operation of a viticultural enterprise. Topics include: organic viticulture, advanced propagation techniques, control of bird management, spray equipment calibration and spray application; pruning, training, trellis erection and repair, propagation, canopy management, physiological pruning, pests and diseases. This course includes visits to commercial vineyards and equipment suppliers.
learning_outcomes: Explain the theory behind pruning and propagation methods and describe how it applies in practice to grape production.
Discuss aspects related to the establishment and re-development of vineyards.
Explain the differences between vineyard management systems and how these differences relate to vineyard sustainability.
Describe the methods used for pest and disease control in viticulture and understand their impact on grape production and quality.
Demonstrate an understanding of how viticultural management can be used to manipulate fruit quality.
Apply key principles and knowledge related to vineyard management to problem solving.
Compose written scientific reports and keep detail lab books on the practical work and field trips undertaken.
antirequisites: must not have completed VITICULT7038WT Viticultural Methods and Procedures at the University of Adelaide

title: Winemaking at Vintage
overview: This course involves teaching sessions that may be attended by both Undergraduate and Postgraduate students. This practical course provides students with the opportunity to gain hands on winemaking experience over the vintage period. The course introduces students to the planning and managing of winemaking strategies. It covers all aspects of grape processing, white juice preparation and red wine fermentation and is designed to complement the theory covered in the other wine technology courses for table wine production. This course also aims to help students make a considerable progression in the developments of their wine sensory evaluation skills.
learning_outcomes: Enhanced their understanding of the winemaking processes.
Become familiar with the operation of vintage machinery.
Gained experience and attain a basic level of competence in routine cellar operations.
Gained an appreciation of the necessity for routine chemical and microbiological analyses during the winemaking process.
Gained experience in cellar safety procedures.
Gained an awareness of the practical organisation required in winery, including the planning of daily winery operations and recording of all such activities.
Gained an appreciation of the importance of organisational skills.
Gained experience in functioning within a teamwork approach.
Critically assess and evalute alternative wine production methods.
prerequisites: must have completed all of WINE5002 Sensory Studies/WINE5005 Introductory Winemaking
antirequisites: must not have completed OENOLOGY7047WT Winemaking at Vintage at the University of Adelaide

title: Viticultural Science B
overview: Viticultural Science B follows on from concepts acquired in Viticultural Science A covering the entire life cycle of the cultivated grapevine. Topics covered in this course include; climate change and its impact on viticulture, berry development and harvesting post-veraison, principles behind the establishment of a viticultural enterprise comprising site selection, choice of planting material, the design and establishment of the vineyard and trellising and canopy management.
learning_outcomes: Decribe the growth cycle of the grapevine and the biology that underpins different phenological stages.
Discuss grapevine physiology as it is relevant to growth and vine form, flowering, water use, mineral nutrition, berry development and ripening.
Describe grapevine anatomy at both the vegetative and reproductive stages.
Apply techniques to monitor grapevine phenological developmental yield potential, canopy modification (pruning) and variety identification.
Understand the taxonomy of grapevines and the characteristics of fruiting varieties.
Employ basic vineyard management practices.
Identify and develop vineyard sites.
Understand the processes involved in the planning, conduct and execution of experimental work.
Describe the role of rootstocks in modern viticultural production.
Work effectively as part of a team and to communicate their understanding and experimental results both verbally and in written form.
prerequisites: must have completed WINE5005 Introductory Winemaking
antirequisites: must not have completed VITICULT7021WT Viticultural Science B at the University of Adelaide

title: Advances in Wine Science
overview: Current research and advanced practices in viticulture and oenology will be examined through lecture/tutorial-based discussion. Viticultural topics will include water relations, water and nutrient use efficiency, climate change, salinity, organic and biodynamic practices and genetic advancement. From an oenological context, emphasis will be placed on grape and wine phenolics and flavour compounds; methods of analysis in wine science; yeast biochemistry, ethanol toxicity, wine stability, yeast aroma compounds; malolactic fermentation. The course will consist of lectures, lab-based practicals, topic debates and a final sensory skill presentation based on sensory skills developed over the course of the Viticulture and Oenology Program.
learning_outcomes: Improved knowledge of current research and advanced practices in viticulture and oenology.
Identify and explain new methods of analysis in wine science, yeast biochemistry and contributions to wine composition, wine stability, malolactic fermentation and fermentation technology.
Critically assess current research in viticulture and oenology.
Describe and critically analyse the sensory characteristics of unknown wines.
Prepare and deliver a consultancy report providing solutions to a viticultural issue faced by the wine industry.
Apply skills developed through prior courses in viticulture and oenology to current industry practice.
prerequisites: must have completed WINE5000 Viticultural Science A
antirequisites: must not have completed OENOLOGY7520WT Advances in Wine Science at the University of Adelaide

title: Experience & Perspectives in the Wine Industry
overview: The Master of Viticulture and Oenology program provides students with opportunities to gain experience working in viticulture and/or winemaking placements. Students undertake 10 weeks work experience, either in an approved viticultural enterprise, and/or in a commercial winery. The placement is normally a continuous 10-week block, taken during the vintage period of the particular region. Viticultural placements, however, may take place throughout the year, and can be composed of a series of discontinuous periods (totalling 10 weeks), enabling students to experience different vineyard practices throughout the year and gain a hands-on working understanding of the management systems and structures. Alternatively students may elect to undertake experience in commercial winery during the vintage period. At the completion of the placement, a specified level of proficiency and an understanding of the contribution of each of the major unit operations to the overall winemaking process are required. In addition students will receive lectures and workshops designed to allow the examination of current policies and issues confronting the Australian wine industry. This will provide insight into how critical Australian wine industry organisations address topics of societal importance, including marketing, wine advertising, brand development and alcohol and health in the international context.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate competency in key practical aspects of work related to commercial grape growing or wine making settings.
Evaluate a range of processes and practices undertaken by commercial grape growing or wine making operations, considering the principles that underpin them.
Evaluate the aims and objectives of the major grape and wine industry organisations.
Analyse issues and challenges that are currently facing the wine industry.
Communicate in both written and oral formats in a professional manner appropriate for the wine industry.
Reflectively analyse placement experiences as they relate to industry issues.
prerequisites: must have completed WINE5007 Winemaking at Vintage
antirequisites: must not have completed WINE6005 Viticulture & Oenology Research Project OR must not have completed OENOLOGY7580WT Experience & Perspectives in the Wine Industry at the University of Adelaide

title: Wine Packaging and Quality Management
overview: This course involves teaching sessions that may be attended by both Undergraduate and Postgraduate students. Science and technology of bottling and packaging systems including chemical and physical properties of packaging materials, principles of filling machinery, design and process control of wine filling/packaging systems. Wine and food laws and commercial forces as quality standards. Taints and residues in grapes and wine as quality issues. Approaches and systems of quality management using the wine industry as a focus, including the development of corporate quality cultures, standards and specifications. Visits will be made to commercial plants.
learning_outcomes: Demonstate an awareness of the physical and chemical properties of packaging materials and how these affect the 'shelf life' of wine.
Understand the principals of filling machines and make correct decisions in matching filling machine types to particular wine types
Demonstrate an awareness of modern packaging materials and products including containers, closures and bottle decorations.
Understand how to prepare a wine for final packaging and have an awareness of how to treat difficult or problem wines prior to packaging.
Understand how modern bottling lines are prepared, operated, monitored and shutdown.
Understand how taints can be caused in wine, how agrochemical maximum residue limits are derived for wine and how taint contaminants and agrochemical residues are assayed in wine
Understand and accept quality management disciplines, techniques and attitudes and how they apply and are increasingly being applied to the wine industry.
prerequisites: must have completed all of WINE5001 Stabilisation and Clarification/WINE5007 Winemaking at Vintage
antirequisites: must not have completed OENOLOGY7004WT Wine Packaging and Quality Management at the University of Adelaide

title: Distillation, Fortified and Sparkling Winemaking
overview: This course involves teaching sessions that may be attended by both undergraduate and postgraduate students. Distillation principles and wine distillation practices. Production of Australian and overseas grape spirits for fortified wine and brandy production. Production of potable distilled beverages other than brandy. Legal requirements of fortified wine production and distillation. Production of Australian and overseas sparkling wine styles. Sensory evaluation of spirits, fortified and sparkling wines.
learning_outcomes: Explain the theory behind distillation and describe how it applies in practice to distillation of feedstocks and production of spirits and fortified beverages.
Critique the methods used to produce fortifying spirits from grape products, and apply principles and calculations relating to distillation and fortification to problem solving.
Discuss aspects related to the legalities and taxation of distilled and fortified beverages in Australia.

Differentiate the methods for producing fortified and sparkling wines, evaluate the quality considerations in their production, and demonstrate an ability to undertake sensory evaluation of spirits, fortifieds and sparkling wines.
Compose written scientific reports based on the practical work undertaken and synthesise scientific information from different sources.
prerequisites: Must have completed all of WINE5002 Sensory Studies/WINE5005 Introductory Winemaking
antirequisites: Must not have completed OENOLOGY 7038WT Distillation, Fortified and Sparkling Winemaking at the University of Adelaide

title: Fermentation Technology
overview: This course involves teaching sessions that may be attended by both Undergraduate and Postgraduate students. This practical course provides students with the opportunity to gain hands on winemaking experience that expands on areas of fermentation technology and preparation of wine for bottling post vintage. The course introduces students to the planning and managing of winemaking strategies, and importantly complements the theory covered in the other wine technology courses for table wine production. Another objective of this course is to help students make a considerable progression in the development of their wine sensory evaluation skills
learning_outcomes: Identify the processes involved in white winemaking
Demonstrate sensory evaluation skills for white wine, beer and cider
Plan, manage and evaluate a winemaking strategy
Produce and critically evaluate a white wine
Apply theories learnt and reflect these in their own white winemaking experiences
Critically assess the production of selected wines and/or regions (PG students only)
prerequisites: must have completed all of WINE5005 Introductory Winemaking/WINE5007 Winemaking at Vintage
antirequisites: must not have completed OENOLOGY7046WT Fermentation Technology at the University of Adelaide

title: Engineering for Viticulture and Oenology
overview: This course aims to provide students with an overview of engineering concepts and applications used in viticulture and wine production. Topics covered within viticulture include irrigation system design, vineyard automation and emerging technologies. Engineering topics related to wine production include: winery design, mass and energy balances, fluid and heat transfer systems, solid separation processes, refrigeration and instrumentation. Practical sessions provide students with an opportunity to apply engineering principles to vineyard and winery operations. Application of experimental design methodologies and engineering process economics is also addressed.
learning_outcomes: Appraise aspects of vineyard and grapevine sensing, irrigation design and scheduling
Describe the application of vineyard automation and advanced technology including robotics and vineyard instrumentation
Explain and communicate via written scientific reports how fundamental principles of process engineering are applied to viticulture and wine production
Apply engineering methodology and safe work practices to winery cellar operations
Employ engineering design principles to assess economic and technical improvement opportunities associated with the operation of a vineyard or winery
prerequisites: must have completed all of WINE5000 Viticultural Science A/WINE5005 Introductory Winemaking
antirequisites: must not have completed OENOLOGY7540WT Engineering for Viticulture & Oenology at the University of Adelaide

title: Wine and Food Retailing
overview: This course addresses the placement of wine and food products into retail channels and examines global distribution systems, multichannel retailing, creating channel partnerships and understanding logistics from the perspective of a wine/food producer. The course also introduces students to the reality of selling into a highly competitive global market. Further, it covers multichannel retail concern through a presentation of distribution channels and strategies and retail metrics to measure retail performance.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse contemporary omnichannel retail contexts and strategies from the perspective of producers, distributors, and retailers across global retail market structures. Articulate management actions and retail planning to address real-life scenarios
Evaluate how producers ultimately engage with consumers through their value chains across the major global market structures of the wine and food industries
Conduct advanced research to inform strategic decision-making and planning processes within the retail sector, demonstrating critical analysis and application of industry-relevant methodologies

Evaluate the significance of product positioning within the retail value chain and develop the capability to deliver concise, well-structured, and visually engaging product pitches tailored to dynamic retail environments
prerequisites: must have completed MARK5010 Marketing for Wine and Food Business
antirequisites: N/A

title: Foundations of Wine Science
overview: Foundations of Wine Science aims to give students an understanding of the basic principles and practices that underpin viticulture (grape production), oenology (wine production) and the technical evaluation of wine sensory profiles. The topics to be covered will include: grape varieties; grapevine structure and function; the annual growth cycle of the grapevine; factors that influence crop yield; the grapevine source/sink balance; berry development and composition; wine classification; the unit operations involved in winemaking; the taste and olfactory system; and aroma and taste interactions. Theoretical content will be supported by practicals that will focus on grapevine anatomy, variety identification and berry ripening, alongside technical wine evaluation (i.e., training in the recognition and evaluation of different wine styles and their characteristic sensory attributes).
learning_outcomes: Describe the morphology, annual growth cycle and fruit development of the grapevine
Understand the photosynthetic process and explain the influence of factors such as light and temperature on photosynthetic activity and grape composition, yield and quality
Outline the processes involved in winemaking that occur before, during and after fermentation, and how these influence wine style and quality
Differentiate the basic sensory processes, their application to technical wine evaluation and the sensory attributes characteristic of different wine styles
Communicate the results of experimental data in written form
antirequisites: Must not have completed BUSI5028 Foundations of Wine Science
assessment: Data Collection and/or Analysis, Data Collection and/or Analysis – 10%

title: UO Problem Solving and Programming
overview: The aim of this course is to develop problem solving skills and basic programming techniques. The aim of this course is topics covered in this course include: a problem solving process, problem solving approaches, data types, variables and constants, Math and Boolean expressions, control structures (sequence, selection and loops), functions and user-defined functions, strings, lists, standard file I/O, and debugging.
learning_outcomes: Explain a problem solving process and computational thinking techniques.
Translate a problem statement into a code solution by following a problem solving process and using computational thinking techniques.
Describe the behaviour and output of algorithms and programs.
Test and debug algorithms and programs.
Demonstrate good programming practices, specifically, coding style standards and source code documentation.
antirequisites: Must not have completed COMP1043 UO Problem Solving and Programming at the University of South Australia OR must not have completed COMP1039 Problem Solving and Programming at the University of South Australia
assessment: Skills Demonstration, Skills Demonstration, Skills Demonstration – 50%

title: UO Object Oriented Programming
overview: The aim of this course is to translate a problem description into a robust object oriented program. The aim of this course is topics covered in this course include: the programming environment, object oriented approaches to program design and development, object concepts and class design, testing, inheritance and polymorphism, and exceptions.
learning_outcomes: Convert a problem statement into an object oriented solution.
Use inheritance and polymorphism to solve problems.
Debug and fix code defects.
Apply international coding style standards.
Plan and conduct testing of software.
Analyse and explain the behaviour of object oriented programs.
prerequisites: must have completed 1 of COMP1021 UO Problem Solving and Programming/COMP1036 Problem Solving and Programming (UniSA)
antirequisites: must not have completed COMP1048 Modelling and Analysis of Complex Systems OR must not have completed COMP1046 Special Topics in Computer Science A
assessment: Skills Demonstration, Skills Demonstration, Skills Demonstration, Skills Demonstration, Skills Demonstration, Skills Demonstration, Skills Demonstration, Skills Demonstration, Skills Demonstration, Skills Demonstration – 60%

title: UO Information Technology Fundamentals
overview: The aim of this course is to develop a solid understanding of core information technology concepts. The aim of this course is topics covered in this course include: historical contexts of computing, computer hardware structure and operation (processors, memory, I/O devices), operating systems and utilities, data representation and number systems, basic concepts required for programming.
learning_outcomes: Discuss IT concepts using appropriate terminology, including history, and current and future trends in IT.
Describe the major components of a computer and operating system.
Apply web programming languages according to features.
Use productivity applications relating to word processors, spreadsheets & presentations.
Describe IT business requirements using UML.
Explain how ethics, privacy & governance impacts information technology.
antirequisites: Must not have completed INFT1024 UO Information Technology Fundamentals at the University of South Australia OR must not have completed INFT1016 Information Technology Fundamentals at the University of South Australia
assessment: Report, Multiple Choice Questions, Skills Demonstration – 60%

title: UO Professional Practice in Data Analytics
overview: The aim of this course is to develop professional practices used in the data analytics industry. The aim of this course is topics covered in this course include: roles in the data analytics community, key phases of the data analytics process, data security, privacy, ethics and cultural awareness.
learning_outcomes: Describe the various roles within the data analytics community.
Identify the development phases of data analytics process and develop skills associated with them.
Identify the privacy and security concerns emerging in contexts using data analytics methods.
Describe how data analytics can impact on indigenous, cultural and diverse groups of people.
Identify stakeholders involved in a data analysis scenario and the means and channels to communicate effectively among them.
Describe the requirements that emerge when working in the context of a data analytics project.
antirequisites: must not have completed INFS1028 UO Professional Practice in Data Analytics at the University of South Australia

title: UO Data Driven Web Technologies
overview: The aim of this course is to construct dynamic websites that utilise queries to retrieve data from a database. The aim of this course is topics covered in this course include: relational databases, structured queries, database design, web technologies and architecture, dynamic website, and web technologies.
learning_outcomes: Explain how data is stored and retrieved from a relational database and the advantages of using the relational mode.
Design a relational database given a set of data and usage requirements.
Implement database queries to retrieve specified data from a relational database.
Construct dynamic webpages using web mark-up languages and data sources.
Describe and discuss the advantages of a range of web architectures.
prerequisites: must have completed all of COMP1021 UO Problem Solving and Programming/INFO1020 UO Information Technology Fundamentals
antirequisites: must not have completed INFT1032 UO Data Driven Web Technologies at the University of South Australia OR must not have completed INFS1025 Data Driven Web Technologies at the University of South Australia
assessment: Problem Solving Task, Problem Solving Task – 50%

title: UO Fundamentals of Mathematics for Data Analytics
overview: The aim of this course is to provide students with the necessary mathematical foundations for a program in data analytics. The aim of this course is topics covered in this course include: arithmetic and algebraic operations, linear equations in one and two variables, quadratic equations, logarithmic and exponential functions, matrices and determinants, absolute value and inequalities, sets, basic probability and statistics.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of foundational mathematics concepts of algebra, key mathematical functions, probability and statistics.
Select and apply appropriate mathematical techniques to solve problems.
Communicate using appropriate mathematical concepts and language.
antirequisites: must not have completed MATH1080 UO Fundamentals of Mathematics for Data Analytics at the University of South Australia

title: UO R for Data Analytics
overview: The aim of this course is to introduce students to the R language and its use for data analysis. The aim of this course is topics covered in this course include: an introduction to descriptive statistics, data description and graphical representation, data manipulation and cleaning, summary measures (centre, spread, skewness, kurtosis, correlation), and exploratory data analysis (EDA) with applications.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate proficiency in the use of core features of the R language.
Use available tools to extract, transform and load data needed for exploratory data analysis.
Perform exploratory data analysis using R.
Effectively use R to present results of exploratory data analysis.
prerequisites: must have completed 1 of COMP1021 UO Problem Solving and Programming/COMP1029 Computer Techniques
antirequisites: must not have completed MATH2032 UO R for Data Analytics at the University of South Australia

title: UO System Requirements and User Experience
overview: The aim of this course is to derive the systems requirements for a given problem statement, and design the user experience for an information technology solution. The aim of this course is topics covered in this course include: introduction to design methodologies, requirements gathering, systems analysis, documenting the requirements, user centered design, user experience, and evaluation and validation.
learning_outcomes: Given a problem statement, identify the key aspects of the users to construct user profiles and assemble the requirements based on stakeholder priorities.
Describe the system requirements following appropriate standards.
Select the requirements to construct the use cases.
Explain a human centred design process.
Apply a human centred design process to document a user interface.
prerequisites: must have completed 1 of COMP1021 UO Problem Solving and Programming/COMP1029 Computer Techniques/INFO1020 UO Information Technology Fundamentals
antirequisites: must not have completed INFS1029 UO System Requirements and User Experience at the University of South Australia OR must not have completed INFS1026 System Requirements and User Experience at the University of South Australia

title: UO Mathematics Essentials in Data Analytics
overview: The aim of this course is to provide students with working knowledge of mathematical and statistical concepts relevant to applications in data analytics. The aim of this course is topics covered in this course include: linear algebra concepts, vectors and matrices operations, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, dynamical systems, optimisation techniques (e.g. Gradient descent), linear regression, probability concepts (probability laws, Bayes' rule and independence), selected probability distributions, statistical inference and applications to data analytics.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate working knowledge of linear algebra, including vectors and matrices to solving problems.
Apply selected optimisation techniques in the context of data analytics.
Apply probability concepts and statistical methods to solving data analytical problems.
Communicate results of mathematical modelling in context of data analytics.
prerequisites: must have completed all of MATH1033 UO Fundamentals of Mathematics for Data Analytics/MATH2018 UO R for Data Analytics
antirequisites: must not have completed MATH1081 UO Mathematics Essentials in Data Analytics at the University of South Australia

title: UO Data Acquisition and Wrangling
overview: The aim of this course is to design ingestion mechanisms from existing databases that prepare data for further analysis. The aim of this course is topics covered in this course include: different data types and formats; regular expressions; web scraping; data exploration, visualisation and preliminary analysis, data profiling and exploratory data analysis; data quality verification, missing data analysis; data wrangling; data cleansing; filtering; sampling; normalisation; visualisations.
learning_outcomes: Assemble requirements and implement processes for data structuring, cleaning, and enrichment via utilising multiple tools.
Identify the alignment required between data collection and analysis.
Design sustainable data management processes that support the analysis and report phases.
Create effective documentation reflecting the structure of data sets prepared for further analysis.
Compare the privacy and ethical implications of sourcing internal and external data.
Perform self-service data preparation.
prerequisites: must have completed 1 of INFO1026 UO Data Driven Web Technologies/INFO1042 Data Driven Web Technologies
antirequisites: must not have completed INFT2067 UO Data Acquisition and Wrangling at the University of South Australia

title: UO Database for the Enterprise
overview: The aim of this course is to provide the skills to interact with existing large sets that are structured or unstructured. The aim of this course is topics in this course include: concurrency and transaction management; data organisation, hash, indexes, query optimisation, active databases, and procedures; distributed database design, fragmentation, and replication; distributed transaction; data warehouse architecture and components; data warehouse modelling: star and snow flake; analysis: multidimensional Online Analytical Processing (OLAP) and relational OLAP; warehouse design, data uploading, updating and integration.
learning_outcomes: Use advanced tools to query and modify structured databases.
Contrast the different types and uses of specialised databases.
Design and use a data warehouses, and select appropriate data processing techniques on the data warehouses.
Design queries to interact with unstructured datasets to retrieve sensible data.
Compare and use data warehousing architectures.
prerequisites: must have completed 1 of INFO1026 UO Data Driven Web Technologies/INFO1042 Data Driven Web Technologies
antirequisites: must not have completed INFT2068 UO Database for the Enterprise at the University of South Australia OR must not have completed INFS2011 Database for the Enterprise at the University of South Australia
assessment: Short Response Questions, Short Response Questions, Short Response Questions – 30%

title: UO Data Visualisation
overview: The aim of this course is to develop skills in data visualisation and communicating with data. The aim of this course is topics in this course include: infrastructure for data visualisation, human side of visualisation, design and construction of visualisation, exploratory approaches to discover insights about data, visualisation for analysis and communication, and visual analytics software.
learning_outcomes: Classify different data types for particular visualisation approaches and select the most appropriate to convey meaning.
Create data visualisations using visualisation software.
Describe and critique common data visualisation approaches to discover insights from data.
Use appropriate data visualisation techniques when exploring data and communicating results of analytics.
prerequisites: Must have completed all of INFO1025 UO System Requirements and User Experience/MATH2018 UO R for Data Analytics
antirequisites: Must not have completed INFS3080 UO Data Visualisation at the University of South Australia OR must not have completed INFS5116 Data Visualisation at the University of South Australia

title: UO Predictive Analytics
overview: The aim of this course is to enable students to perform data exploration, visualisation, and analysis using predictive modelling techniques. The aim of this course is topics covered in this course include: classification: naive bayes, decision trees, SVM, Neural Networks, random forest, ensemble; regression: linear, logistic; model evaluation, overfitting, pruning.
learning_outcomes: Develop accurate predictive models based on large data sets.
Perform predictive analytics on large data sets using an industry standard software tool-set.
Communicate appropriately with professional colleagues through visualisation and report.
Select and implement supervised machine learning techniques that are appropriate for the applications under consideration.
Select suitable model parameters for different supervised machine learning techniques.
prerequisites: must have completed all of MATH1034 UO Mathematics Essentials in Data Analytics/MATH2018 UO R for Data Analytics
antirequisites: must not have completed INFS3081 UO Predictive Analytics at the University of South Australia OR must not have completed INFS5100 Predictive Analytics at the University of South Australia

title: UO Applied Data Structures
overview: The aim of this course is to develop skills in selecting and implementing appropriate data structures and algorithms to develop software to solve problems. The aim of this course is topics covered in this course include: the programming environment; integrated development environments, commenting and the JavaDoc tool; the Java API; inheritance; interfaces and abstract classes; polymorphism; use of Inheritance in advanced data structures; exceptions and exception handling; fundamental algorithms (searching, sorting, hash tables, binary search trees, representing graphs, graph traversals, shortest path, transitive closure, minimum spanning tree, topological sorting, simple numerical algorithms, string and pattern matching); advanced file IO: NIO, object serialisation.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the capability to evaluate algorithms, to select from a range of options, to provide justification for the selection, and to implement the algorithm in a programming context.
Apply strategies (problem-solving techniques) to conceptualise problems, and formulate a solution, including mapping the solution to classes within the Java programming language.
Debug and fix code defects.
Communicate appropriately with professional colleagues through source code documentation.
prerequisites: Must have completed 1 of COMP1023 UO Object Oriented Programming/COMP1038 Object Oriented Programming (UniSA)
antirequisites: Must not have completed COMP2033 UO Applied Data Structures at the University of South Australia

title: UO Cloud Platforms
overview: The aim of this course is to provide a detailed overview of cloud concepts, AWS core services, security, architecture, pricing and support, and how these can be used by an organisation to support their IT infrastructure. The aim of this course is topics covered in this course include: overview of cloud concepts, cloud models IaaS, PaaS, SaaS; introduction to AWS, AWS Global Infrastructure; Cloud Security: Identity and Access Management (IAM), Security Policy; Networking: Virtual private clouds (VPC) vs public clouds; architectural principles of cloud computing; Core Cloud Services: EC2, Lambda, S3; and other cloud service offerings from Azure and Google Cloud.
learning_outcomes: Describe the different types of cloud computing models.
Compare the benefits of cloud computing with traditional on-premises.
Identify the most appropriate cloud-base service to meet a specific need.
Apply a range cloud-based services including security, networking, compute, and storage.
Construct a working cloud IT infrastructure based on an existing on-premise design.
prerequisites: must have completed INFO1020 UO Information Technology Fundamentals
antirequisites: must not have completed INFT2066 UO Cloud Platforms at the University of South Australia OR must not have completed INFT2069 Cloud Platforms at the University of South Australia

title: UO Critical Approaches to Online Learning
overview: The aim of this course is to prepare Adelaide University Online students for successful online study through the development of knowledge, skills and affective qualities that promote success in higher education. This course is designed to prepare students for success in the Adelaide University Online learning environment. Students will investigate a topic related to the future challenges of their discipline area, which will help to prepare for further study and graduate careers. Students will learn how to summarise academic articles, critically analyse texts, generate ideas, interpret data, and images and other supporting material for academic studies, write a report, demonstrate academic integrity and reference sources of information. The course will introduce many relevant digital tools and explore how these can be used to conduct research, complete online assessments and more. The skills and approaches learned throughout this course will help prepare students for success in undergraduate programs.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate critical management and use of digital technology and information
Apply skills and knowledge in the use of communications tools and media for collaborative learning
Understand the University academic integrity policy and apply principles of academic integrity in academic work
Demonstrate self-awareness and build resilience as learners
Demonstrate skills in the identification and analysis of real-world issues using academic approaches
antirequisites: must not have completed CURR3021 UO Critical Approaches to Online Learning at the University of South Australia
assessment: Assignment, Assignment, Multiple Choice Questions, Multiple Choice Questions – 60%

title: UO Introduction to Engineering Chemistry
overview: The aim of this course is to introduce students to the basic concepts of chemistry as they relate to engineering and to provide them with some experience of virtual practical work to the theory in the course. Practical and theoretical studies of properties of matter; physical and chemical changes; atoms, elements and compounds; structure and bonding; acids, bases and salts; redox; precipitation reactions; the mole; heat of reactions; metals, non-metals and their compounds. Periodic Table. Introduction to main engineering aspects of organic chemistry.
learning_outcomes: Interpret relevant basic physical chemistry processes
Recall the basics of chemical structure and bonding in ionic and molecular species
Identify basic chemistry procedures, including titration, purification, gravimetric and lab safety
antirequisites: Must not have completed ENGG1006 UO Introduction to Engineering Chemistry at the University of South Australia OR must not have completed CHEM1015 Introduction to Engineering Chemistry at the University of South Australia

title: UO Essential Mathematics 1: Algebra and Trigonometry
overview: The aim of this course is to increase confidence and ability in mathematical skills, to provide an introduction to the understanding of mathematical principles of algebra and trigonometry, and to introduce systematic problem solving techniques. A review of basic algebra; introduction to algebraic functions and their graphs; trigonometric functions, properties and identities; elementary theory of matrices and linear algebra.
learning_outcomes: Apply elementary manipulative skills to solve mathematical problems
Formulate simple applied problems in mathematical language
Use the principles of elementary trigonometry and linear algebra in the solution of problems
antirequisites: must not have completed MATH1076 UO Essential Mathematics 1 - Algebra and Trigonometry at the University of South Australia OR must not have completed MATH1066 Essential Mathematics 1 - Algebra and Trigonometry at the University of South Australia
assessment: Multiple Choice Questions, Multiple Choice Questions, Multiple Choice Questions, Multiple Choice Questions – 40%
Problem Solving Task, Data Collection and/or Analysis, Oral Defence – 60%

title: UO Essential Mathematics 2: Calculus
overview: The aim of this course is to increase confidence and ability in mathematical skills, to provide an introduction to the understanding of mathematical principles of differential and integral calculus, and to introduce systematic problem solving techniques. Exponential and logarithmic functions; differential calculus; integral calculus.
learning_outcomes: Calculate derivatives of functions using first principles arguments.
Apply rules of differentiation to find derivatives of more complex functions generated by products, quotients and composition.
Formulate simple problems involving related rates and optimisation in mathematical language.
Use the principles of elementary differential and integral calculus to solve applied problems involving rates and areas.
prerequisites: must have completed 1 of MATH1029 UO Essential Mathematics 1: Algebra and Trigonometry/MATH1056 Essential Mathematics 1: Algebra and Trigonometry
antirequisites: must not have completed MATH1077 UO Essential Mathematics 2 - Calculus at the University of South Australia OR must not have completed MATH1067 Essential Mathematics 2 - Calculus at the University of South Australia
assessment: Multiple Choice Questions, Multiple Choice Questions, Problem Solving Task, Problem Solving Task – 50%

title: UO Sustainable Engineering Practice
overview: The aim of this course is to introduce students to the engineering profession through course and project work and interaction with industry. All are designed to help students to develop some of the essential personal and professional skills needed for sustainable professional practice. Course resources will introduce students to a variety of areas in sustainable and professional engineering, including the role of the professional engineer, graduate attributes of engineering professionals, career management skills, critical analysis and reflective practice, principles of sustainable engineering, professional ethics, intercultural issues including Indigenous protocols, basic project management principles, effective teamwork, team roles, evaluation of team performance, engineering report writing, effective presentations, locating and using information and referencing.
learning_outcomes: Describe the role of the civil, electrical, and mechanical engineer in modern society.
Reflect on and demonstrate self-awareness of strengths and weaknesses relative to the attributes of professional engineers.
Demonstrate an awareness of the socio-cultural, safety, ethical, global and sustainable contexts in which engineering is practised.
Develop a solution to an engineering problem using inclusive teamwork skills and applying basic project management principles.
Demonstrate professional oral, written and visual communication skills appropriate for engineering practice.
antirequisites: must not have completed ENGG1007 UO Sustainable Engineering Practice at the University of South Australia OR must not have completed ENGG1003 Sustainable Engineering Practice at the University of South Australia

title: UO Mathematical Methods for Engineers 1
overview: The aim of this course is to provide an introduction to mathematical concepts relevant to engineering disciplines using both analytic and software approaches. Introduction to the computer software program MATLAB and its applications.Definition and properties of vectors, applications to the geometry of the plane, complex numbers, operations on complex numbers, modulus and its properties, functions and their graphs with applications to trigonometric, exponential, logarithmic and inverse functions, differentiation and applications to related rates problems and to maxima and minima problems, l'Hôpital's rule, parametric representation of curves, solution of simple differential equations, visualisation of motion using computer software, integration of trigonometric and rational functions with applications to the calculation of simple plane areas and rates of change.
learning_outcomes: Apply vector methods to problems in two and three dimensional spaces
Apply trigonometric functions; differentiate and integrate trigonometric, exponential, logarithmic and rational functions and extend the results to engineering applications
Sketch and graph functions, with emphasis on trigonometric functions
Express curves describing movement in parametric form
Investigate motion using appropriate computer software
Find and interpret both definite and indefinite integrals
Report on findings in both simple tasks and projects
prerequisites: must have completed 1 of MATH1030 UO Essential Mathematics 2: Calculus/MATH1051 Essential Mathematics 2: Calculus
antirequisites: must not have completed MATH1078 UO Mathematical Methods for Engineers 1 at the University of South Australia OR must not have completed MATH1063 Mathematical Methods for Engineers 1 at the University of South Australia

title: UO Mathematical Methods for Engineers 2
overview: The aim of this course is to develop and extend mathematical concepts relevant to mechanical, civil and electrical engineering using both analytic and software approaches. the course includes Applied Linear Algebra Vectors and matrices, linear dependence of vectors, linear systems of equations, row operations as matrix multiplications, row reduced echelon form (RREF), matrix inverse, determinants, eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a square matrix, degenerate eigenvalues, diagonalisation of a square matrix, application to coupled systems of ordinary differential equations with examples from mechanics and ecology. MATLAB exercises. Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs) and Techniques of Integration Linear and separable differential equations of first order. Inverse trigonometric functions and their derivatives, hyperbolic functions. Techniques of integration: Integration by parts, integration using partial fractions, trigonometric integrals, trigonometric substitutions. Improper integrals. Applications of integration in mechanics: area, volume of regular bodies, centre of mass, moment of inertia, work. Linear differential equations of second order: reduction of order, homogenous and inhomogeneous equations, constant coefficient ODEs, applications in mechanics and electrical circuits. MATLAB exercises.
learning_outcomes: apply elementary manipulative skills to solve mathematical problems
formulate simple applied problems in mathematical language
use the principles of linear algebra in the solution of problems selected from engineering
use the principles of differential and integral calculus in the solution of problems selected from engineering
solve simple applied problems using MATLAB software
prerequisites: must have completed 1 of MATH1031 UO Mathematical Methods for Engineers 1/MATH1047 Mathematical Methods for Engineers 1
antirequisites: must not have completed MATH1079 UO Mathematical Methods for Engineers 2 at the University of South Australia OR must not have completed MATH1064 Mathematical Methods for Engineers 2 at the University of South Australia
assessment: Multiple Choice Questions, Problem Solving Task, Problem Solving Task – 55%

title: UO Introduction to Engineering Physics
overview: The aim of this course is to introduce students to a study of the physical world and to develop their knowledge and understanding of some of the basic laws and principles of physics and their practical applications to engineering. Scalars and vectors; force and motion; energy and momentum; rotational motion and gravity; solids and fluids; vibrations and waves; electricity and magnetism.
learning_outcomes: Explain relevant physical phenomena clearly and accurately in the appropriate terminology.
Relate basic laws and principles of physics to practical applications in engineering.
Express well-defined relationships between physical quantities as formulae.
Accurately perform calculations on a range of problem-solving exercises.
Analyse, process and accurately present experimental data obtained from physics experiments or simulations.
antirequisites: Must not have completed PHYS1019 UO Introduction to Engineering Physics at the University of South Australia OR must not have completed PHYS1018 Introduction to Engineering Physics at the University of South Australia
assessment: Skills Demonstration, Skills Demonstration, Skills Demonstration – 50%

title: UO Programming Concepts
overview: The aim of this course is to develop problem solving skills and core programming techniques to acquire and process real-world data related to civil, electrical, mechanical and other engineering problems. This course allows students to develop an understanding of fundamental programming concepts and the relevance of programming in solving engineering problems. These concepts will be applied through design and implementation of programming code and the use of microcontrollers. The course also covers coding standards and good programming practices, as well as problem solving processes and tools. Programming concepts covered in this course include: representing data (data types, variables, constants); math and Boolean expressions (relational, equality and Boolean operators); control constructs (sequence, selection, iteration); using and writing functions (call by value and call by reference); arrays (1-D and 2-D); strings; pointers; dynamic memory allocation; structures; array of structures; multi-file programs; standard and file input and output. Programming integrated development environments (for both C and microcontrollers) will be used.
learning_outcomes: Apply problem solving strategies to move from a problem statement to a code solution.
Implement, test and debug programs using the C programming language and choose appropriate conditional and iteration constructs for a given programming task.
Analyse and explain the behaviour of programs.
Program a microcontroller to perform a simple task relevant to a civil, electrical, mechanical or other engineering problem.
Apply good programming practices, specifically, international coding style standards and source code documentation.
antirequisites: Must not have completed COMP1045 Programming Concepts at the University of South Australia OR must not have completed COMP1047 UO Programming Concepts at the University of South Australia
assessment: Skills Demonstration, Skills Demonstration, Oral Defence – 70%

title: UO Engineering Design and Innovation
overview: This course provides opportunities for students to build and extend a range of personal and professional skills. They will solve practical engineering design problems and recognise the roles of systems thinking, innovation and creativity in the design process. This course will help students to develop visual communication skills such as understanding and producing 2D engineering drawings and 3D engineering models. Course resources will introduce students to the exciting and complex world of engineering design and innovation. Activities and projects will help students to explore engineering problem solving, basic systems engineering concepts, creativity tools, engineering design process, project management principles, professional reflections, principles of safe design, link between ethics and creativity, and developing oral, written, and visual communication skills. This course will develop 2D and 3D visualisation skills and engineering drawing skills, which are essential to communicate designs while meeting industry drawing standards.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the civil, electrical, and mechanical engineering design process and the Australian Standard for technical drawing AS1100.
Develop visualisation and drawing skills and construct 2D drawings and 3D solid models to communicate design.
